addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

## claude.ai Dropbox
# Claude App MCP LLM Boot Instructions

You are the assistant for Dropbox's Claude App MCP server. Your goal is to help users complete Dropbox tasks quickly and correctly while minimizing friction.

## Customer Use Cases

This app is best at helping users do these Dropbox workflows:

- Browse folder contents and paginate through large directories.
- Find files quickly using plain-language search terms and then open files with follow-on tools.
- Inspect file metadata (size, type, timestamps, IDs, sharing context).
- Check signed-in Dropbox identity, team/account context, and namespace-root context.
- Read text content from supported files up to 5 MiB, and provide a usable Dropbox link even when text extraction fails.
- Generate single-use temporary download links when the user explicitly needs direct file download URLs.
- Generate file previews with thumbnail and "open in Dropbox" experiences.
- Create folders in the right destination before saving artifacts.
- Create new text files directly in Dropbox.
- Create share links for files/folders and return the effective sharing settings.
- Inspect and list existing shared links.
- List, inspect, and create Dropbox file requests.
- Move, rename, copy, and delete Dropbox files/folders after explicit confirmation.
- Check the status of long-running move, copy, and delete jobs.

When users ask "what can you do?", summarize these use cases in plain language before taking action.

## Not Supported (Do Not Advertise)

- Editing or overwriting existing file content in place.
- Saving URL-hosted files directly into Dropbox.
- Uploading local/binary artifacts via `upload_file`.
- Permanent file deletion or wipe workflows. `delete` moves items to the user's Dropbox "Deleted files" area only.
- Reliable text extraction for supported files via `fetch`; extraction may still fail for some files, in which case the tool error may include a usable link.
- E-signature initiation or signing workflows.
- Actions outside Dropbox content management and sharing.

## Core Behavior

## devonthink
CRITICAL — Database package safety: DEVONthink databases are stored as packages (.dtBase2) or sparse images (.dtSparse, .dtArchive). Never modify, rename, move, or delete files inside a database package directly via the filesystem. All record and content operations must go through this MCP server or, as a fallback, via AppleScript. Direct filesystem manipulation will corrupt the database and cause irreversible data loss.

Batch operations: Use the uuids array parameter instead of sequential single-record calls for tag, update, move, trash, duplicate, replicate, and export operations. Batch mode is faster, reduces round trips, and returns a summary with succeeded/failed counts.

Avoiding duplicates: Use lookup_records (by name, URL, path, filename, or comment) before create_record to check whether a record already exists.

Content editing: Prefer update_record_content with mode append or insert over replace for large documents. Replace mode requires sending the entire new content and risks accidental data loss if the content is incomplete.

Group hierarchies: Use create_group_path to create nested group structures in a single call (like mkdir -p) rather than sequential create_record calls.

AI-powered tools: classify_record and find_similar_records use DEVONthink's built-in AI algorithms and proprietary training data — they provide organizational suggestions that complement, not duplicate, your own capabilities.

Record enrichment: resolve_doi_metadata and resolve_book_metadata can enrich existing records with bibliographic metadata by passing the record's uuid — there is no need to create a new record.

AI exclusion: Records marked as excluded from AI access (excludeFromChat) are protected in two ways. (1) Input protection: any tool that receives such a record's UUID as an argument refuses to operate on it and returns an error. (2) Output protection: result lists from tools like search_records, classify_record, find_similar_records, get_record_children, get_record_duplicates, and the link traversal tools are filt… [truncated]

## omnifocus
OmniFocus is a GTD task manager. Hierarchy: Folders > Projects > Tasks > Subtasks.

TASK STATES: Available, Blocked, Deferred (future defer date), Flagged, Overdue, Completed, Dropped. Planned Date is a scheduling signal only — no availability/overdue constraints.

PROJECT TYPES: "sequential" (tasks in order; first incomplete = available, rest blocked; position = dependencies), "parallel" (all available), "single_actions" (no completion goal, cannot auto-complete). The `next` field is true for the first available action in a sequential project/action group; in parallel projects, all incomplete tasks have `next: true`.

ACTION GROUPS: Task with subtasks. Parent shows `blocked: true` while subtasks are active — this is normal, not an error. Do not try to unblock it.

INHERITED STATUS: `completed`/`dropped` reflect the task's own state, not its container's. `effectivelyCompleted`/`effectivelyDropped` reflect the container's state — if true, the task's parent project or action group was completed/dropped. Task in completed project: `completed: false`, `effectivelyCompleted: true`, `available: false`. Use `available_only=True` for actionable tasks.

EFFECTIVE DATES: Dates returned by get_tasks are always effective (inherited). A task with no direct due date WILL show its project's due date in the dueDate field — this is correct behavior, not a bug. You cannot clear an inherited date at the task level. Write operations set the task's own date.

RECURRING TASKS: `completed=True` uses `mark complete`, which creates the next occurrence. This is guaranteed. WARNING: Dropping a recurring task (status='dropped') without clearing recurrence first (recurrence='') spawns the next occurrence. To stop a series: update_tasks([{"id": "...", "recurrence": "", "status": "dropped"}]).

TAGS: Represent work contexts. Tag statuses: Active (normal), On Hold (tasks excluded from Available perspective), Dropped (tag hidden from picker; does NOT affect task availability).

DEFER vs DUE: Defer = hidden until that date. Due = deadline.

- codebase-design: Shared vocabulary for designing deep modules. Use when the user wants to design or improve a module's interface, find deepening opportunities, decide where a seam goes, make code more testable or AI-navigable, or when another skill needs the deep-module vocabulary.
- diagnosing-bugs: Diagnosis loop for hard bugs and performance regressions. Use when the user says "diagnose"/"debug this", or reports something broken/throwing/failing/slow.
- domain-modeling: Build and sharpen a project's domain model. Use when the user wants to pin down domain terminology or a ubiquitous language, record an architectural decision, or when another skill needs to maintain the domain model.
- find-skills: Helps users discover and install agent skills when they ask questions like "how do I do X", "find a skill for X", "is there a skill that can...", or express interest in extending capabilities. This skill should be used when the user is looking for functionality that might exist as an installable skill.
- grilling: Grill the user relentlessly about a plan or design. Use when the user wants to stress-test a plan before building, or uses any 'grill' trigger phrases.
- prototype: Build a throwaway prototype to answer a design question. Use when the user wants to sanity-check whether a state model or logic feels right, or explore what a UI should look like.
- research: Investigate a question against high-trust primary sources and capture the findings as a Markdown file in the repo. Use when the user wants a topic researched, docs or API facts gathered, or reading legwork delegated to a background agent.
- seo-optimizer: Optimize content for search engines with keyword analysis, readability scoring, meta descriptions, and competitor comparison. Use this when users want to improve SEO, optimize blog posts, or analyze content for search performance.
- systems-thinking: Analyze problems using a Systems Thinking approach. Use when users mention "systems thinking," "systemic," "feedback loops," "unintended consequences," "root cause," "interconnected," or request analysis of complex, multi-factor problems. Guides conversation through questions and observations rather than prescriptive solutions.
- tdd: Test-driven development. Use when the user wants to build features or fix bugs test-first, mentions "red-green-refactor", or wants integration tests.
- add-backlinks: Add backlinks from related blog posts and glossary entries to a target post. Use when the user wants to improve internal linking by having other content link back to a specific article.
- blog-post: Create or revise a blog post for the Agile Pain Relief website. Use when the user wants to write a new blog post, revise/refresh an existing one, or update content. Guides through gathering information, content structure, internal linking, and post-publish steps.
- evergreen-posting: Compile Mark's selected social drafts into the batch JSON the posting pipeline consumes (LinkedIn / Mastodon / Bluesky), validating character limits and URL budgets, threading the link when it won't fit, and marking the source calendars so nothing is promoted twice. Blog/glossary/newsletter prose is authored and selected UPSTREAM as Markdown via the vault linkedin-style draft skill; this skill condenses the selected options to three platforms and writes the JSON, it does not re-draft that prose. Quiz posts are still drafted here from seeds. Use when Mark says "build the batch JSON", "compile the selected drafts", "schedule social media", or asks for the evergreen batch.
- glossary-entry: Create a new glossary term for the Agile Pain Relief website. Use when the user wants to add a new Agile/Scrum term definition, concept explanation, or methodology entry to the glossary.
- indexing-strategy: Use this skill when Mark asks to analyze, plan, or implement SEO topic clusters and internal linking for agilepainrelief.com. Covers two modes: (1) ANALYZE mode — audit existing content, identify pillar/cluster opportunities, find gaps and orphaned pages, and produce a prioritized action plan; (2) IMPLEMENT mode — generate specific internal linking instructions, write or revise blog posts and glossary entries to fit the cluster strategy, and produce per-page checklists. Also use when Mark asks what a blog post or glossary entry needs for SEO, or when he wants to check whether a draft meets the cluster linking requirements.
- newsletter: Draft and send a newsletter to the Newsletter Subscribers list via Cakemail, starting from plain markdown. Use when Mark wants to write, render, test, or dispatch a newsletter / email campaign, or turn a markdown file into a Cakemail draft campaign. Drives the email-automation CLI's send-newsletter command.
- social-media-adapt: Adapt LinkedIn posts to Mastodon and Bluesky formats with platform-specific character limits, thread formatting, and JSON structure. Use when Claude needs to convert LinkedIn content to other social platforms, create threaded posts, or adapt content for different character limits (Mastodon 500 chars, Bluesky 290 chars).
- claude-md-management:revise-claude-md: Update CLAUDE.md with learnings from this session
- claude-md-management:claude-md-improver: Audit and improve CLAUDE.md files in repositories. Use when user asks to check, audit, update, improve, or fix CLAUDE.md files. Scans for all CLAUDE.md files, evaluates quality against templates, outputs quality report, then makes targeted updates. Also use when the user mentions "CLAUDE.md maintenance" or "project memory optimization".
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

title: 'Which parts of the Scrum Master job still need a person?'
description: 'Eight quick questions about how you actually spent the last couple of Sprints. See which parts of your role are getting more valuable, and which parts the tools are starting to do.'
resultStyle: 'map-move'
# The email is asked for after the last question, before the map. The cover says
# so up front (heroButtonNote + intro), so nobody is ambushed by the ask; the
# trade is volume at the top of the funnel for people who finish the questions.
capturePosition: 'end'
# Shuffle each question's answers so the slipping/mixed/gaining/context order
# never telegraphs the "best" pick.
randomizeOptions: 'shuffle'

heroHeading: 'Which parts of the Scrum Master job still need a person?'
heroBody: 'Eight quick questions about how you actually spent the last couple of Sprints. See which parts of the work are getting more valuable, and which parts the tools are starting to do. Works whether you hold the title, cover it alongside delivery work, or run the process as a project manager.'
heroButtonLabel: 'Start the quiz'
# States the email ask on the cover, right under the button that starts the quiz.
heroButtonNote: 'Free, and about three minutes. You’ll add your email address after the last question, before I show you your map.'
# Labels the button that finishes the quiz, which here is the capture form's.
submitButtonLabel: 'Show me my map'

# The cover's three-step strip: what the taker gets, shown before the opt-in.
howItWorks:
  - label: 'step 1'
    title: 'Answer 8 questions'
    body: 'I’ll ask your role first, then eight questions about your last couple of Sprints. Answer honestly.'
    icon: 'steps'
    tone: 'accent'
  - label: 'step 2'
    title: 'See your map'

  - label: 'step 3'

introHeading: 'Before you start'

intro: |
  This isn’t a test. There’s no right answer, no score, and nobody else sees what you pick, not your manager, not your team. Take a moment and think about the last couple of Sprints your team had, and when you answer, take the time to think about what actually happened.

  The quiz is here to help you think about the role and find a way to improve. After the last question I’ll ask for your email address, and then you get your map.

categoriesHeading: 'The three parts of the role this maps'

persuasion: |
  This isn’t a personality quiz. I hate those too. I won’t sugarcoat the challenges, but I do recognize that you work in the real world.

persuasionBullets:
  - 'Free'
  - 'Eight quick questions, about three minutes'
  - 'Immediate results, no waiting'
  - 'The work getting more valuable, and the work the tools are starting to do'
  - 'Clear, honest recommendations you can act on'
  - 'No archetype, no score for the wall, no gobbledygook'

captureBody: 'That was the last question. Add your email address and I’ll show you your map.'

captureFootnote: 'You’ll also join my email list for Scrum Masters navigating GenAI. No spam. Unsubscribe anytime.'

## Radar/spider charts on results pages

Radar charts work best with enough dimensions to look meaningful: the radar or spider chart displays ratings that relate to each other — for example results across 5 dimensions — and it's ideal for 5 dimensions or higher, since below that the chart loses visual appeal. Some tools (e.g., Evalinator) even let you show a live chart of average results so far on the landing page, with the chart type selectable in Landing Page Options.

Native support isn't universal, though. A Typeform community thread shows someone building a personality quiz with seven categories, each rated 1–10, wanting to display results in a radar graph and asking whether it's even possible. The practical outcome: they used a workaround with a simple scale on the end screen, noting that products doing "that fancy stuff" are expensive and the form was meant to be a free lead magnet.

## Archetype classifiers

Archetype results are mainly a segmentation device: map each result to a tailored resource, a focused offer, or a nurture path matching that archetype. Real-world example: Alissa Boyer promoted "The Intuitive Queen" — one result from her Sensitive Strength Archetype Quiz — with custom illustration and a trait description, since showing an actual result up front previews what people get.

One caution on question count: very short archetype quizzes can feel like a waste of time because they don't ask enough questions to produce an accurate result — relevant if you want a defensible multi-dimensional score behind a radar chart.

## Assessment vs. personality framing

Assessment quizzes are diagnostic, identifying gaps, risks, or maturity levels; they suit consultants, agencies, and high-ticket offers where lead quality beats volume, and highlighting underperformance creates a natural opening for audits or strategy calls. Look for software that gives a score plus personalised feedback — a "Discover your fitness personality!" quiz sounds fun but delivers little insight, whereas a scored "Body Transformation Scorecard" rates their actual diet and exercise routine. For B2B buyers or high-stakes decisions, use the words "quiz" or "assessment" in your headings and copy.

## Tooling notes

- **ScoreApp** — segmentation tools let you follow up with targeted emails or route people to the most relevant product pages.
- **Quiz and Survey Master (WordPress)** — dynamic result pages based on scores or answers plus redirects, with integrations to Mailchimp, ConvertKit, ActiveCampaign, Zapier, and Google Sheets.
- **Evalinator** — the only result here explicitly offering radar as a built-in chart type.

## The gap worth noting

Nothing in these results covers a single tool doing all three well — radar visualization *plus* archetype classification *plus* lead capture. The Typeform thread suggests that combination typically requires either a specialized assessment platform or a custom results page. If you want, I can search specifically for tools with native radar chart output or for custom results-page implementations.

Here's what the search turned up on team agility assessments with radar-chart output:

## Comparative Agility (CA)The Comparative Agility assessment tool was developed by Kenny Rubin, Mike Cohn, and Dr. Laurie Williams, and is used to help organizations assess their agility relative to other organizations or teams that responded to the tool. It is a survey-based assessment tool. Practitioners can visit the CA website, answer the survey questions, and receive a free report comparing their results against the industry dataset, with answers recorded on a five-point Likert scale. Customized surveys can also be requested. At the highest level, CA identifies seven dimensions forming the basis of the agility assessment — comparable to the Key Process Areas of CMM/CMMI.

## AgilityHealth Radar (TeamHealth Radar)The TeamHealth Radar is AgilityHealth's most popular assessment for measuring the health and maturity of Agile teams. It measures team health across 5 dimensions, is typically completed by Product Owners, Scrum Masters, Technical Leads and team members, and is run once a quarter or at the end of a release/PI.AgilityHealth Radar is also the primary endorsed SAFe assessment tool, built through a formal partnership with Scaled Agile. The radar chart format visualizes results across all domains at once, making it easy to see which behaviors are well-established versus underdeveloped, and benchmark data aggregated from thousands of assessments across the AgilityHealth community lets you contextualize results against similar organizations.

## Team radar charts generallyA team radar (also called a spider diagram) is a visual assessment tool for evaluating performance, capabilities or health across multiple dimensions simultaneously, creating a polygon where each axis is a metric scored from the center (low) to the outer edge (high). Each team member individually rates the team on a 1–5 scale, usually during retrospectives or dedicated health-check sessions. Benefits include data-driven improvement discussions, progress tracking via comparative overlays, and shared alignment on team capabilities.

## Free / low-cost alternatives
- **TeamRetro** offers health-check radars, including one focused on agile development practices used sprint to sprint, covering requirements and risk, design and coding, and testing and deployment.
- **Echometer** combines agility health checks with retrospectives, letting validated KPIs be measured regularly in small pulse surveys; a sample retro can be opened without logging in.
- **NextAgile** provides a free Agile Maturity Assessment template with questionnaire, scoring model, and radar chart, plus guidance on survey design, stakeholder alignment, radar chart analysis, and growth plan creation.

**Bottom line:** For a genuinely free benchmarked report, Comparative Agility's public survey is the classic option; AgilityHealth's TeamHealth Radar is the enterprise/SAFe-endorsed choice (demo-based rather than free), and TeamRetro, Echometer, and template-based approaches cover the lightweight DIY end.

Here's what the search turned up on team agility assessments with radar-chart output:

## Comparative Agility (CA)The Comparative Agility assessment tool was developed by Kenny Rubin, Mike Cohn, and Dr. Laurie Williams, and is used to help organizations assess their agility relative to other organizations or teams that responded to the tool. It is a survey-based assessment tool. Practitioners can visit the CA website, answer the survey questions, and receive a free report comparing their results against the industry dataset, with answers recorded on a five-point Likert scale. Customized surveys can also be requested. At the highest level, CA identifies seven dimensions forming the basis of the agility assessment — comparable to the Key Process Areas of CMM/CMMI.

## AgilityHealth Radar (TeamHealth Radar)The TeamHealth Radar is AgilityHealth's most popular assessment for measuring the health and maturity of Agile teams. It measures team health across 5 dimensions, is typically completed by Product Owners, Scrum Masters, Technical Leads and team members, and is run once a quarter or at the end of a release/PI.AgilityHealth Radar is also the primary endorsed SAFe assessment tool, built through a formal partnership with Scaled Agile. The radar chart format visualizes results across all domains at once, making it easy to see which behaviors are well-established versus underdeveloped, and benchmark data aggregated from thousands of assessments across the AgilityHealth community lets you contextualize results against similar organizations.

## Team radar charts generallyA team radar (also called a spider diagram) is a visual assessment tool for evaluating performance, capabilities or health across multiple dimensions simultaneously, creating a polygon where each axis is a metric scored from the center (low) to the outer edge (high). Each team member individually rates the team on a 1–5 scale, usually during retrospectives or dedicated health-check sessions. Benefits include data-driven improvement discussions, progress tracking via comparative overlays, and shared alignment on team capabilities.

## Free / low-cost alternatives
- **TeamRetro** offers health-check radars, including one focused on agile development practices used sprint to sprint, covering requirements and risk, design and coding, and testing and deployment.
- **Echometer** combines agility health checks with retrospectives, letting validated KPIs be measured regularly in small pulse surveys; a sample retro can be opened without logging in.
- **NextAgile** provides a free Agile Maturity Assessment template with questionnaire, scoring model, and radar chart, plus guidance on survey design, stakeholder alignment, radar chart analysis, and growth plan creation.

**Bottom line:** For a genuinely free benchmarked report, Comparative Agility's public survey is the classic option; AgilityHealth's TeamHealth Radar is the enterprise/SAFe-endorsed choice (demo-based rather than free), and TeamRetro, Echometer, and template-based approaches cover the lightweight DIY end.

I read the engine, the `map-move` renderer, and the `scrum-master-ai` frontmatter, and looked at both examples you linked. Here's what I found, then the decisions I need from you before I build.

**What the examples actually do** (they're all the same recipe):

- **Practical PKM Flywheel** — 5 named stages (Capture / Curate / Connect / Cultivate / Create), radar shows the shape, the *lowest* axis is highlighted as "your bottleneck", and the archetype name ("The Hoarder") is derived from that bottleneck. Numbers appear in the bars below, not on the radar.
- **STTI (LYT)** — 4 archetype axes (Synthesizer / Producer / Inner Guide / Creative) plus two tendency spectra, archetype label "IS-Architect / The Philosopher", radar plus a numeric score breakdown.

**Two more in the same genre**, both closer to your domain:

- **[Comparative Agility](https://www.comparativeagility.com/)** (Cohn, Rubin, Laurie Williams) — 7 dimensions, free survey, radar report benchmarked against the industry dataset. The benchmark ("you vs. everyone else") is the pull, not an archetype.
- **[AgilityHealth TeamHealth Radar](https://agilityhealthradar.com/team-health-radar-assessment/)** — 5 dimensions, the SAFe-endorsed one, radar is literally the product name. Enterprise/demo rather than free.
- Lighter-weight, if you want to see the mechanic without enterprise pricing: **[TeamRetro's health-check radars](https://www.teamretro.com/health-checks/development-practices-health-check-radar/)** and the **[Color Personality Test](https://www.colorpersonalitytest.net/your-color-personality-profile/)** (4 dimensions → percentage dashboard → one of 8 archetypes; the clearest cheap example of dimensions-to-classifier).

**The problem I have to flag before building.** `scrum-master-ai` today has 8 scored questions across 3 sections (time / coaching / system), scored 0/1/2. A 3-axis radar is a triangle, and an 8-axis radar has only three possible positions per spoke, so it comes out spiky rather than meaningful. Neither reads like your examples. Separately, `MapMoveResults.astro` and the engine README both record "no number, letter or tier title anywhere" as a hard requirement, and `context` answers (part-time role, no Product Owner) deliberately score 0 so they're *never* counted as a gap. A radar plots them as a low point, which is the exact thing that design refused. Your call to reverse, but I want it to be a decision rather than a side effect.

questions.question: What should the radar's axes be?

options.label: 5 dimensions, 2 questions each (Recommended)
options.description: Restructure the quiz's 3 sections into 5 named dimensions and add 2 questions (8 → 10). Gives a pentagon like the Flywheel example, and each spoke has 5 positions instead of 3 so the shape means something. Costs: new section copy, 2 new questions, and the cover's "eight questions" wording changes in 4 places.

options.label: 3 axes = the existing sections
options.description: time / coaching / system. No content change at all, ships fastest. But it draws a triangle, and with uneven question counts per section (3/3/2) it needs normalising to percentages. Visually the weakest of the three.

options.label: 8 axes, one per question
options.description: An octagon with no content change. Each spoke is a single 0/1/2 question, so the outline is jagged and the axis labels are long question stems that have to be abbreviated.

questions.question: Does the radar bring the classifier back with it?

options.label: Radar + archetype name, no numbers (Recommended)
options.description: Keep the "map, not grade" rule for numbers, but name the taker from their weakest spoke the way the Flywheel names "The Hoarder". Keeps the one recommended move as the payoff. The archetype is what makes these quizzes shareable.

options.label: Radar only, no archetype, no numbers
options.description: Purely swaps the balance bar for a radar and changes nothing else. Fully consistent with the current design rules. Least pull, but zero copy rewrite.

options.label: Full classifier: archetype + per-axis score bars
options.description: Match the examples exactly: archetype headline, radar, then numeric bars per dimension with the bottleneck called out. Most persuasive and most shareable, but reverses the no-score decision outright and needs archetype copy written for each bottleneck.

questions.question: How should a 'context' answer plot on the radar (part-time role, no Product Owner to coach)?

options.label: Plot low, but annotate the axis (Recommended)
options.description: Draw it at its real 0 so the shape is honest, and mark that spoke as constrained (dashed segment plus a line in the existing context strip) so it reads as "outside your control", not "you failed".

options.label: Exclude the axis entirely
options.description: Drop the spoke from the polygon and grey the label. Nobody is blamed for something structural, but the radar changes shape between takers, which makes it harder to read and impossible to compare.

options.label: Score it as mid, not zero
options.description: Treat a context answer as neutral so it neither rewards nor penalises. Simplest to implement and keeps the polygon regular, but it quietly hides a real problem the current design goes out of its way to surface.

1	import { type SchemaContext } from 'astro:content';
2	import { z } from 'astro/zod';
3	
4	/**
5	 * Returns a Zod schema for a quiz content collection entry. Designed to be
6	 * called from the function-form `schema:` callback of `defineCollection` so
7	 * the Astro `image()` helper can be threaded through to image-bearing fields.
8	 *
9	 *   import { createQuizSchema } from '@/lib/quiz-engine';
10	 *
11	 *   const quizzes = defineCollection({
12	 *     loader: glob({ pattern: '**\/*.mdx', base: './src/content/quizzes' }),
13	 *     schema: (ctx) => createQuizSchema(ctx),
14	 *   });
15	 *
16	 * Consumers can `.extend()` the returned schema to add site-specific fields
17	 * without touching the engine.
18	 */
19	export function createQuizSchema({ image }: SchemaContext) {
20	  const threshold = z.object({
21	    level: z.string(),
22	    minScore: z.number().int().nonnegative(),
23	    maxScore: z.number().int().nonnegative(),
24	    title: z.string().optional(),
25	  });
26	
27	  // Copy + selection config for the `map-move` result style. Everything here is
28	  // generic (no site-specific wording is baked into the engine); the author
29	  // supplies the strings in frontmatter and the `MapMoveResults` component
30	  // renders them around the computed map. Only used when `resultStyle` is
31	  // `'map-move'`.
32	  const mapMove = z.object({
33	    // Question ids in priority order. The `reclaim` move points at the
34	    // highest-priority question whose chosen answer is in the `slipping`
35	    // bucket; `redirect` does the same over its own ordered list.
36	    reclaimPriority: z.array(z.string()).default([]),
37	    redirectPriority: z.array(z.string()).default([]),
38	    eyebrow: z.string().optional(),
39	    // The result heading. Keep it descriptive: this style never grades anyone,
40	    // so no tier title and no archetype here.
41	    heading: z.string().optional(),
42	    opening: z.string().optional(),
43	    // Label above the balance bar (the lead visual: proportion, never a score).
44	    balanceLabel: z.string().optional(),
45	    gainingHeading: z.string(),
46	    // Shown in the gaining/slipping columns when that column is empty.
47	    gainingEmpty: z.string().optional(),
48	    slippingHeading: z.string(),
49	    slippingEmpty: z.string().optional(),
50	    moveHeading: z.string().optional(),
51	    contextHeading: z.string().optional(),
52	    // Body shown instead of the reclaim/redirect move when nothing is slipping.
53	    wellPositioned: z.string().optional(),
54	    // Body shown when nothing was decisive enough to point at (every answer in
55	    // the middle). Omit it and the payoff block is dropped rather than rendered
56	    // as an empty box.
57	    noMove: z.string().optional(),
58	    close: z.string().optional(),
59	    // Light, descriptive framing line above the map. The engine picks one of
60	    // the three based on the ratio of gaining to slipping answers. Never an
61	    // archetype or score.
62	    framing: z
63	      .object({
64	        gaining: z.string(),
65	        mixed: z.string(),
66	        slipping: z.string(),
67	      })
68	      .optional(),
69	    // Footer row: one line of secondary text plus an accent link.
70	    cta: z
71	      .object({
72	        body: z.string().optional(),
73	        buttonLabel: z.string(),
74	        buttonHref: z.string(),
75	      })
76	      .optional(),
77	  });
78	
79	  return z.object({
80	    title: z.string(),
81	    description: z.string().optional(),
82	    intro: z.string().optional(),
83	    resultsSubtitle: z.string().optional(),
84	    // Selects the results-rendering strategy. `'band'` (default) maps a total
85	    // score into a level and renders `<ResultCard>` blocks. `'map-move'`
86	    // renders a per-answer map plus one recommended move (see `mapMove`).
87	    resultStyle: z.enum(['band', 'map-move']).default('band'),
88	    // Where the email capture sits. `'end'` (default) asks after the last
89	    // question; `'start'` makes it a hard gate before question 1. A start gate
90	    // runs before anything is answered, so `levelTagPrefix` has no result to
91	    // tag with and is ignored.
92	    capturePosition: z.enum(['start', 'end']).default('end'),
93	    // Cover strip showing what the taker gets, before they hand anything over.
94	    // Each chip is tinted by `tone` purely for warmth and sequence.
95	    howItWorks: z
96	      .array(
97	        z.object({
98	          label: z.string().optional(),
99	          title: z.string(),
100	          body: z.string().optional(),
101	          icon: z.string().optional(),
102	          tone: z
103	            .enum(['accent', 'valuable', 'slipping', 'alt'])
104	            .default('accent'),
105	        })
106	      )
107	      .optional(),
108	    sections: z
109	      .array(
110	        z.object({
111	          id: z.string(),
112	          label: z.string(),
113	          blurb: z.string().optional(),
114	          image: image().or(z.string()).optional(),
115	        })
116	      )
117	      .min(1),
118	    questions: z
119	      .array(
120	        z.object({
121	          id: z.string(),
122	          section: z.string(),
123	          text: z.string(),
124	          reveal: z.string().optional(),
125	          // Small text above the question, in place of the section label.
126	          label: z.string().optional(),
127	          // 'profile' classifies the taker instead of assessing them: no score,
128	          // no map entry, no progress, always asked first. Use it to set an
129	          // option's `tag` and/or `lens`.
130	          kind: z.enum(['scored', 'profile']).optional(),
131	          options: z
132	            .array(
133	              z.object({
134	                text: z.string(),
135	                score: z.number().int(),
136	                // Concept icon shown beside this answer's sentence in the map.
137	                icon: z.string().optional(),
138	                // map-move classification. `context` marks a real-world
139	                // constraint (e.g. part-time role) that must NOT be counted as
140	                // a gap. Ignored by the band style.
141	                bucket: z
142	                  .enum(['gaining', 'mixed', 'slipping', 'context'])
143	                  .optional(),
144	                // The line shown for this answer in the map (gaining column,
145	                // slipping column, or the context notes). Omit for `mixed`.
146	                mapSentence: z.string().optional(),
147	                // Shown when this answer is selected as the reclaim / redirect
148	                // target of the one move.
149	                reclaimSentence: z.string().optional(),
150	                redirectSentence: z.string().optional(),
151	                // Tag applied to the submission when this answer is chosen.
152	                tag: z.string().optional(),
153	                // Standing instruction shown from the moment this answer is
154	                // chosen and above every later question, for answers that change
155	                // who the rest of the quiz is about.
156	                lens: z.string().optional(),
157	              })
158	            )
159	            .min(2),
160	        })
161	      )
162	      .min(1),
163	    // Band-style scoring bands. Optional so `map-move` quizzes can omit them.
164	    sectionLevels: z.array(threshold).min(1).optional(),
165	    overallLevels: z.array(threshold).min(1).optional(),
166	    mapMove: mapMove.optional(),
167	    randomize: z.enum(['none', 'within-sections']).default('none'),
168	    // Controls the order options are shown in within a question. `'shuffle'`
169	    // randomizes them per visit so a fixed slipping→mixed→gaining→context order
170	    // never telegraphs the "best" answer. Scoring is keyed by the option's
171	    // original index, so this affects presentation only.
172	    randomizeOptions: z.enum(['none', 'shuffle']).default('none'),
173	  });
174	}

1 # Astro Quiz Engine 2 3 A small, self-contained quiz engine for Astro sites. Quiz content lives in MDX 4 files under a content collection; the engine provides the schema, the scoring 5 helpers, a React stepper component, and a results-page primitive. 6 7 The engine is intentionally generic. It has no opinion about: 8 9 - where the user lands afterward (you provide the `onSubmit` callback) 10 - where leads go (CRM, email tool, JSON file, whatever) 11 - what the level labels mean ("high-risk", "tier-1", "beach" -- all opaque 12 strings to the engine) 13 - styling beyond Tailwind utility classes 14 15 ## Quick start 16 17 ### 1. Register the content collection 18 19 ```ts 20 // src/content.config.ts 21 import { defineCollection } from 'astro:content'; 22 import { glob } from 'astro/loaders'; 23 import { createQuizSchema } from '@/lib/quiz-engine'; 24 25 const quizzes = defineCollection({ 26 loader: glob({ pattern: '**/*.mdx', base: './src/content/quizzes' }), 27 schema: (ctx) => createQuizSchema(ctx), 28 }); 29 30 export const collections = { quizzes /* + your others */ }; 31 ``` 32 33 `createQuizSchema` follows the [`SchemaContext`](https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/modules/astro-content/) pattern used by Starlight and recommended in the Astro docs: it receives the schema context (which carries Astro's `image()` helper) so section images can be content-relative paths that get optimized through Astro's asset pipeline. The returned Zod object can be `.extend()`ed with site-specific frontmatter fields: 34 35 ```ts 36 schema: (ctx) => 37 createQuizSchema(ctx).extend({ 38 heroHeading: z.string().optional(), 39 }), 40 ``` 41 42 ### 2. Author a quiz in MDX 43 44 ```mdx 45 --- 46 title: 'How GenAI Fails in Software Teams' 47 intro: 'Twelve questions. Three minutes.' 48 sections: 49 - id: delivery 50 label: 'Delivery & Outcomes' 51 blurb: 'What happens when AI code reaches production.' 52 questions: 53 - id: q1 54 section: delivery 55 text: 'In the METR study, senior devs using AI on familiar code were:' 56 reveal: 'Self-reported productivity is unreliable.' 57 options: 58 - { text: '20% faster', score: 0 } 59 - { text: 'about the same', score: 0 } 60 - { text: '19% slower', score: 1 } 61 - { text: '50% slower', score: 0 } 62 sectionLevels: 63 - { level: 'high-risk', minScore: 0, maxScore: 0 } 64 - { level: 'low-risk', minScore: 1, maxScore: 1 } 65 overallLevels: 66 - { level: 'high-risk', minScore: 0, maxScore: 0, title: 'High Risk' } 67 - { level: 'low-risk', minScore: 1, maxScore: 1, title: 'Low Risk' } 68 randomize: within-sections # optional; defaults to 'none' 69 --- 70 71 import ResultCard from '@/lib/quiz-engine/components/ResultCard.astro'; 72 73 74 ### Delivery & Outcomes 75 You haven't seen the METR study yet. 76 77 78 79 ### Delivery & Outcomes 80 You already know perceived productivity outruns real productivity. 81 82 ``` 83 84 ### 3. Render the stepper on a landing page 85 86 ```astro 87 --- 88 // src/pages/quiz/[slug].astro 89 import { getEntry } from 'astro:content'; 90 import QuizStepper from '@/lib/quiz-engine/components/QuizStepper'; 91 92 const entry = await getEntry('quizzes', Astro.params.slug); 93 if (!entry) return Astro.redirect('/404'); 94 --- 95 96 102 ``` 103 104 Scoring happens in the browser via `computeQuizResult` + `buildResultQuery` from 105 the engine. On submit, the stepper assembles `email`, `custom_attributes[firstname]`, 106 and any tags as multipart form-data, delivers them (see below), then redirects to 107 `/quiz/{slug}/results/?...` with the locally-computed query string. 108 109 **Delivery is pluggable. Provide EITHER:** 110 111 - `cakemailFormUrl?: string` — built-in path. POSTs the form-data straight to a 112 Cakemail hosted-form action URL with `mode: 'no-cors'` (fire-and-forget). This 113 is best-effort: a network error is logged but the user still reaches their 114 results. Good for a simple standalone setup. 115 - `onSubmit?: (formData: FormData) => Promise` — host owns delivery. Receives 116 the assembled form-data; route it through your own endpoint (e.g. a CAPTCHA-gated 117 proxy, or any ESP). Unlike the built-in path this hook is **authoritative**: if it 118 throws, the engine shows the thrown message and keeps the user on the capture step 119 to retry; resolve to proceed to results. If both are supplied, `onSubmit` wins. 120 121 To mount a widget the host needs at submit time (e.g. a CAPTCHA whose token your 122 `onSubmit` reads), pass it via: 123 124 - `captureExtras?: React.ReactNode` — rendered inside the capture form, just above 125 the submit button. Opaque to the engine. 126 127 > APR uses these to gate the quiz behind Cloudflare Turnstile: a wrapper supplies 128 > `captureExtras={}` and an `onSubmit` that appends the token and POSTs 129 > to a server endpoint, keeping this engine free of Turnstile/ESP specifics. 130 131 Two optional props drive audience tagging, sent as Cakemail's `tags[]=true` 132 form fields alongside the email: 133 134 - `submissionTags?: string[]` — static tags applied to every submission (e.g. 135 `['aiquiz']`). Use these as the segment an ESP automation triggers on. 136 - `levelTagPrefix?: string` — when set, also tags `${levelTagPrefix}${overallLevel}` 137 (e.g. `'aiquiz-'` + a computed level `'high-risk'` => `aiquiz-high-risk`), so a 138 nurture sequence can branch on the result tier. 139 140 Note: the tag field names follow Cakemail's hosted-form convention. With `onSubmit` 141 you can remap them to any ESP before sending. 142 143 Capture copy is overridable so it can read correctly wherever the step sits: 144 `captureHeading`, `captureBody`, `captureButtonLabel` (the capture form's own 145 button) and `captureFootnote`. `submitButtonLabel` is a separate prop: it labels 146 whichever button *finishes* the quiz and goes to the results. 147 148 Keep those two straight. On a start gate the capture button leads to question 1, 149 so it defaults to `startButtonLabel`; a finish label there ("See my results") 150 promises something the next screen doesn't deliver. 151 152 ### 4. Render the results 153 154 ```astro 155 --- 156 // src/pages/quiz/[slug]/results.astro 157 export const prerender = false; 158 import { getEntry, render } from 'astro:content'; 159 160 const entry = await getEntry('quizzes', Astro.params.slug); 161 if (!entry) return Astro.redirect('/404'); 162 const { Content } = await render(entry); 163 --- 164 165

Your results

166

Score: {Astro.url.searchParams.get('total')} / {Astro.url.searchParams.get('max')}

167 168 169 ``` 170 171 The `` blocks inside the MDX body check the URL search params and 172 render only when the requested section/level matches. 173 174 `` takes `section` and `level` (both required) plus an optional 175 `image`. Pass an imported `ImageMetadata` (preferred, so Astro optimizes it) or 176 a plain URL string to show a small icon atop the card. A common pattern is to 177 reuse the same per-section icons from the landing page so the results mirror it: 178 179 ```mdx 180 import ResultCard from '@/lib/quiz-engine/components/ResultCard.astro'; 181 import deliveryIcon from './images/delivery.png'; 182 183 184 ### Delivery & Outcomes 185 You haven't seen the METR study yet. 186 187 ``` 188 189 ## Public API 190 191 ```ts 192 import { 193 // schema 194 createQuizSchema, 195 196 // pure scoring 197 computeQuizResult, 198 buildResultQuery, 199 findLevel, 200 getOptionScore, 201 getMaxQuestionScore, 202 203 // true for questions that count toward the score, map and progress 204 isScored, 205 206 // types 207 type QuizData, 208 type QuizQuestion, 209 type QuizQuestionKind, 210 type QuizSection, 211 type QuizLevelThreshold, 212 type QuizResponses, 213 type QuizResult, 214 } from '@/lib/quiz-engine'; 215 216 import QuizStepper from '@/lib/quiz-engine/components/QuizStepper'; 217 import ResultCard from '@/lib/quiz-engine/components/ResultCard.astro'; 218 ``` 219 220 ## Result styles 221 222 A quiz picks its results renderer with the `resultStyle` frontmatter field 223 (defaults to `'band'`): 224 225 - **`'band'`** — the total score maps to an overall level, and the results page 226 renders the `` blocks that match (everything above). 227 Use for knowledge or risk quizzes with a "you scored X, you're a Y" result. 228 - **`'map-move'`** — no single band. Each answer is classified into a bucket, and 229 the results page renders a two-column map (work getting more valuable vs. work 230 slipping away) plus one recommended move. Submitting 297 delivers the contact and redirects to the results. 298 - **`'start'`** — the capture form as a **hard gate**, then the intro, then the 299 questions. Submitting delivers the contact and advances; the last question's 300 button is what finishes the quiz. The taker knows up front that an email is 301 involved, and it self-qualifies for higher intent at the cost of some volume. 302 The gate renders as a compact, **email-only** panel (no first-name field: 303 every extra field on a gate costs completions), so it can sit inside the host 304 page's cover layout rather than replacing it. 305 306 Whichever comes first is the step the host page's marketing chrome sits 307 alongside, so hide that chrome on `index !== 0` from `quiz:step-changed` rather 308 than keying on the step's `kind`. 309 310 Two consequences of a start gate worth knowing: 311 312 - **`levelTagPrefix` does nothing.** Nothing has been answered at submit time, 313 so there is no result tier to tag with. Static `submissionTags` still apply. 314 - **The contact is delivered before the quiz is finished.** Someone who gates in 315 and then abandons at question 3 is on your list without a result. That's the 316 trade the position makes; if you need the result to reach the ESP, capture at 317 the end. 318 319 Back-navigating onto an already-submitted gate does not re-deliver the contact; 320 the button just moves the taker forward. 321 322 ## Profile questions 323 324 A question with `kind: 'profile'` classifies the **taker** instead of assessing 325 them. It is not part of the assessment, so it: 326 327 - contributes nothing to the score, the section scores, or the map; 328 - carries no progress bar and is excluded from the progress total, so a cover 329 that promises "eight questions" stays true when you add one; 330 - always leads, in declared order, ahead of anything `randomize` does; 331 - keeps its declared option order even under `randomizeOptions: 'shuffle'`, 332 because there is no "best" pick to hide and role lists have their own order. 333 334 Give it a `section` id that **isn't** one of your declared sections, so it adds 335 no card to the landing page's section list. Nothing then supplies the eyebrow 336 text above the question, so set `label` — otherwise it is the only screen in the 337 quiz with nothing above the heading, and nothing to tell the taker it isn't one 338 of the questions the cover promised. `score` is still required on each option 339 (the field is not optional); use `0` and ignore it. 340 341 Its two payloads are per-option: 342 343 ```yaml 344 - id: role 345 section: profile 346 kind: profile 347 label: 'Before the eight questions' 348 text: 'Which of these roles best describes what you do?' 349 options: 350 - text: 'Scrum Master. It’s the job I’m hired to do.' 351 score: 0 352 tag: 'role-scrum-master' 353 - text: 'Manager. I manage the Scrum Master, or the team, or both.' 354 score: 0 355 tag: 'role-manager' 356 lens: 'Answering as a manager: think about where your Scrum Master spent their time, not where you spent yours.' 357 ``` 358 359 **`tag`** is applied to the submission when that answer is chosen, sent as 360 `tags[]=true` alongside the host's static `submissionTags`. Scoring is keyed by question `id`, so randomization affects 497 presentation only. 498 499 The optional `randomizeOptions` field controls option order *within* a 500 question: 501 502 - `'none'` (default): show options in the declared order. 503 - `'shuffle'`: randomize the options per visit, so a fixed 504 slipping/mixed/gaining/context (or wrong/right) order never telegraphs the 505 "best" answer. Decided once on mount; scoring is keyed by each option's 506 original index, so shuffling is presentation-only. 507 508 Each option carries an a/b/c/d chip lettered by its **display** position. Using 509 the authored letter would both come out jumbled once shuffled (b, d, a, c) and 510 leak the authoring pattern, e.g. that "d" is always the `context` answer. The 511 chip anchors the eye and carries no meaning, so it is `aria-hidden`. 512 513 **Picking never advances the step.** The taker chooses, then presses the button. 514 Auto-advance would be one tap rather than two, but it takes the answer away 515 before they can reconsider, which is wrong for a quiz asking someone to think 516 back over several weeks, and it moves keyboard and screen-reader users without 517 warning (WCAG 3.2.2, On Input). 518 519 ## Roadmap (when this is extracted) 520 521 - Ship as an Astro integration with `injectRoute` so consumers don't have to 522 write landing/results pages by hand 523 - Optional signed query strings on the results URL 524 - Per-section level threshold overrides (right now `sectionLevels` applies 525 to all sections uniformly) 526 - Optional `correctOption` field on questions so the stepper can mark 527 right/wrong inline without inferring from `score` 528

Quiz content lives in MDX files under a content collection; the engine provides the schema, the scoring helpers, a React stepper component, and a results-page primitive. The engine is intentionally generic. It has no opinion about: - where the user lands afterward (you provide the `onSubmit` callback) - where leads go (CRM, email tool, JSON file, whatever) - what the level labels mean ("high-risk", "tier-1", "beach" -- all opaque strings to the engine) - styling beyond Tailwind utility classes ## Quick start ### 1. Register the content collection ```ts // src/content.config.ts import { defineCollection } from 'astro:content'; import { glob } from 'astro/loaders'; import { createQuizSchema } from '@/lib/quiz-engine'; const quizzes = defineCollection({ loader: glob({ pattern: '**/*.mdx', base: './src/content/quizzes' }), schema: (ctx) => createQuizSchema(ctx), }); export const collections = { quizzes /* + your others */ }; ``` `createQuizSchema` follows the [`SchemaContext`](https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/modules/astro-content/) pattern used by Starlight and recommended in the Astro docs: it receives the schema context (which carries Astro's `image()` helper) so section images can be content-relative paths that get optimized through Astro's asset pipeline. The returned Zod object can be `.extend()`ed with site-specific frontmatter fields: ```ts schema: (ctx) => createQuizSchema(ctx).extend({ heroHeading: z.string().optional(), }), ``` ### 2. Author a quiz in MDX ```mdx --- title: 'How GenAI Fails in Software Teams' intro: 'Twelve questions. Three minutes.' sections: - id: delivery label: 'Delivery & Outcomes' blurb: 'What happens when AI code reaches production.' questions: - id: q1 section: delivery text: 'In the METR study, senior devs using AI on familiar code were:' reveal: 'Self-reported productivity is unreliable.' options: - { text: '20% faster', score: 0 } - { text: 'about the same', score: 0 } - { text: '19% slower', score: 1 } - { text: '50% slower', score: 0 } sectionLevels: - { level: 'high-risk', minScore: 0, maxScore: 0 } - { level: 'low-risk', minScore: 1, maxScore: 1 } overallLevels: - { level: 'high-risk', minScore: 0, maxScore: 0, title: 'High Risk' } - { level: 'low-risk', minScore: 1, maxScore: 1, title: 'Low Risk' } randomize: within-sections # optional; defaults to 'none' --- import ResultCard from '@/lib/quiz-engine/components/ResultCard.astro'; ### Delivery & Outcomes You haven't seen the METR study yet. ### Delivery & Outcomes You already know perceived productivity outruns real productivity. ``` ### 3. Render the stepper on a landing page ```astro --- // src/pages/quiz/[slug].astro import { getEntry } from 'astro:content'; import QuizStepper from '@/lib/quiz-engine/components/QuizStepper'; const entry = await getEntry('quizzes', Astro.params.slug); if (!entry) return Astro.redirect('/404'); --- ``` Scoring happens in the browser via `computeQuizResult` + `buildResultQuery` from the engine. On submit, the stepper assembles `email`, `custom_attributes[firstname]`, and any tags as multipart form-data, delivers them (see below), then redirects to `/quiz/{slug}/results/?...` with the locally-computed query string. **Delivery is pluggable. Provide EITHER:** - `cakemailFormUrl?: string` — built-in path. POSTs the form-data straight to a Cakemail hosted-form action URL with `mode: 'no-cors'` (fire-and-forget). This is best-effort: a network error is logged but the user still reaches their results. Good for a simple standalone setup. - `onSubmit?: (formData: FormData) => Promise` — host owns delivery. Receives the assembled form-data; route it through your own endpoint (e.g. a CAPTCHA-gated proxy, or any ESP). Unlike the built-in path this hook is **authoritative**: if it throws, the engine shows the thrown message and keeps the user on the capture step to retry; resolve to proceed to results. If both are supplied, `onSubmit` wins. To mount a widget the host needs at submit time (e.g. a CAPTCHA whose token your `onSubmit` reads), pass it via: - `captureExtras?: React.ReactNode` — rendered inside the capture form, just above the submit button. Opaque to the engine. > APR uses these to gate the quiz behind Cloudflare Turnstile: a wrapper supplies > `captureExtras={}` and an `onSubmit` that appends the token and POSTs > to a server endpoint, keeping this engine free of Turnstile/ESP specifics. Two optional props drive audience tagging, sent as Cakemail's `tags[]=true` form fields alongside the email: - `submissionTags?: string[]` — static tags applied to every submission (e.g. `['aiquiz']`). Use these as the segment an ESP automation triggers on. - `levelTagPrefix?: string` — when set, also tags `${levelTagPrefix}${overallLevel}` (e.g. `'aiquiz-'` + a computed level `'high-risk'` => `aiquiz-high-risk`), so a nurture sequence can branch on the result tier. Note: the tag field names follow Cakemail's hosted-form convention. With `onSubmit` you can remap them to any ESP before sending. Capture copy is overridable so it can read correctly wherever the step sits: `captureHeading`, `captureBody`, `captureButtonLabel` (the capture form's own button) and `captureFootnote`. `submitButtonLabel` is a separate prop: it labels whichever button *finishes* the quiz and goes to the results. Keep those two straight. On a start gate the capture button leads to question 1, so it defaults to `startButtonLabel`; a finish label there ("See my results") promises something the next screen doesn't deliver. ### 4. Your results

Score: {Astro.url.searchParams.get('total')} / {Astro.url.searchParams.get('max')}

It appears under the options the moment that answer is picked, and again above every later question. Reach for it when an answer changes *who the remaining questions are about*: a manager taking a quiz whose every question says "you" will otherwise answer about their own week and get a map of the wrong job. The repeat is the point — a one-off note at question 0 is forgotten by question 3. The profile answer does ride along in the `map-move` results query, so a results page can branch on it later; the built-in renderer ignores it. ## Look and feel The engine ships one visual system rather than raw Tailwind defaults, because a quiz reads as a single artefact. Two rules drive it: - **Colour encodes meaning, never decoration.** Four roles: `valuable`, `slipping`, `context`, `accent` (the recommendation). Colour is always backed by an icon, a label and a position, so nothing is lost in greyscale or to colour-blindness. Slipping is amber, never red: red reads as failure, and these quizzes don't grade anyone. - **Flat surfaces.** White cards with hairline borders, tinted panels with none, no gradients and no shadows. The one exception is the map-move "one move" callout, which gets a 2px accent border because it's the payoff. Type is serif headings (`font-heading`) over sans body, two weights only (400 and 500), sentence case throughout, in a ~680px reading column. > **Known issue (TODO):** the current quiz components aren't consistently using > the project's canonical Tailwind classes. Audit the component markup and bring > the utility classes in line with the site's conventions before this is treated > as done. The host site supplies the palette as CSS custom properties, so restyling a quiz means redefining tokens rather than editing components. Define all of these (APR's live in `src/styles/global.css`): ``` --color-quiz-page --color-quiz-valuable-tint --color-quiz-slipping-tint --color-quiz-card --color-quiz-valuable-strong --color-quiz-slipping-strong --color-quiz-hairline --color-quiz-valuable-edge --color-quiz-slipping-edge --color-quiz-ink --color-quiz-accent-tint --color-quiz-context-panel --color-quiz-ink-secondary --color-quiz-accent-strong --color-quiz-step3-tint --color-quiz-ink-muted --color-quiz-accent-edge --color-quiz-step3-strong ``` ### Icons Quizzes name icons by *concept* (`icon: 'admin'`), not by an icon library's name. `components/QuizIcon.tsx` maps those concepts onto a real icon family and is the only file that knows which one, so swapping art families is a one-file change and no frontmatter moves. The vocabulary: `time`, `admin`, `people`, `productOwner`, `root`, `system`, `handsOn`, `impediment` for concepts, plus `steps`, `map`, `next`, `privacy`, `gaining`, `slipping` for the engine's own chrome. An unknown name renders nothing rather than throwing, since the icon is always reinforcement and never the only carrier of meaning. APR currently maps these to Lucide. ### Cover "how it works" strip Optional `howItWorks` frontmatter renders a row of cards showing what the taker gets, which matters most when the capture is a start gate: they see the offer before they hand anything over. ```yaml howItWorks: - label: 'step 1' title: 'Answer 8 questions' body: 'Think back over your last couple of sprints.' icon: 'steps' tone: 'accent' # accent | valuable | slipping | alt ``` `tone` is warmth and sequence only, deliberately separate from the semantic roles the result page uses. ## Design notes **Scoring is data-driven.** Each option carries a numeric `score`. For knowledge quizzes, use `0` for wrong and `1` for the correct option. For spectrum quizzes (where every answer earns something), use whatever weights you like. The engine sums them. **Level labels are opaque strings.** The engine doesn't know that "high-risk" is bad. It just maps total/section scores into bands and exposes the matched level so your content can branch on it. Rename your bands without touching engine code. **The results page is stateless.** All computed values live in the URL query string. That means results pages are shareable, bookmarkable, and survive a refresh -- but it also means anyone can craft a URL to view a tier. If you need tamper-resistance, sign the query string in the API endpoint and verify on the results page. **The stepper handles browser history.** Each step pushes a `history.pushState` entry, and a `popstate` listener restores the step index. The back button walks the user through the quiz, not out of it. **Answers are changeable unless picking one gave something away.** An answer locks only when the pick disclosed something the taker could act on: a quiz with `showCorrectness`, or a question carrying `reveal` copy. That stops someone "fixing" a knowledge score after seeing the right answer. A reflective question discloses nothing, so its options stay live and re-pickable, and because responses are keyed by question id the back button lets the taker revise earlier answers too. **Events.** The stepper dispatches two output events on `window`: - `quiz:step-changed` — `{ kind: 'intro' | 'question' | 'capture', index: number }` on every transition. Use it to react to navigation (e.g. hide marketing chrome once the user leaves the intro step). - `quiz:started` — one-shot, fires the first time the user leaves the intro. Intended for analytics. On a start-gated quiz that is when the gate appears, not when question 1 does; use `quiz:step-changed` if you need to separate "saw the gate" from "passed it". It also listens for one input event: - `quiz:start-requested` — advances past the intro step if the stepper is currently on it. Lets a host page's own marketing chrome ("Start the Quiz" hero button, etc.) trigger the quiz without reaching into the React island. **Question order.** The optional `randomize` frontmatter field controls how questions are presented: - `'none'` (default): show questions in the order declared in frontmatter. - `'within-sections'`: preserve the declared section order, but shuffle the questions inside each section. The user still moves through sections in the same sequence; only the within-section order varies per visit. Order is decided once on mount and stays stable across re-renders and the back button. Scoring is keyed by question `id`, so randomization affects presentation only. The optional `randomizeOptions` field controls option order *within* a question: - `'none'` (default): show options in the declared order. - `'shuffle'`: randomize the options per visit, so a fixed slipping/mixed/gaining/context (or wrong/right) order never telegraphs the "best" answer. Decided once on mount; scoring is keyed by each option's original index, so shuffling is presentation-only. Each option carries an a/b/c/d chip lettered by its **display** position. Using the authored letter would both come out jumbled once shuffled (b, d, a, c) and leak the authoring pattern, e.g. that "d" is always the `context` answer. The chip anchors the eye and carries no meaning, so it is `aria-hidden`. **Picking never advances the step.** The taker chooses, then presses the button. Auto-advance would be one tap rather than two, but it takes the answer away before they can reconsider, which is wrong for a quiz asking someone to think back over several weeks, and it moves keyboard and screen-reader users without warning (WCAG 3.2.2, On Input). ## Roadmap (when this is extracted) - Ship as an Astro integration with `injectRoute` so consumers don't have to write landing/results pages by hand - Optional signed query strings on the results URL - Per-section level threshold overrides (right now `sectionLevels` applies to all sections uniformly) - Optional `correctOption` field on questions so the stepper can mark right/wrong inline without inferring from `score`

Three visuals it is. One last thing to settle, because it's the real cost of this change and it might move your pick.

Neither axis exists in the data today:

- **Trajectory** (is this work appreciating or depreciating) is nowhere in the frontmatter. It's stated in your prose — "that's the part GenAI can't replace", "that's the work GenAI is already starting to take" — but never as a value anything can plot.

Which matters because the Transfer visual needs almost none of this, the trajectory axis needs one new number per question, and the Quadrant needs both.

Mockup is open in your browser: `temp/quiz-result-visuals.html`. Three visuals × two answer profiles (the admin-buried full-timer, and the part-timer whose answers are half `context`). No source files touched.

**A real bug fell out of modelling your data.** `q2` sits first in `redirectPriority`, but `q2`'s slipping answer (the status-and-logistics desk) has no `redirectSentence` — only a `reclaimSentence`. `eligible()` in `map-move.ts:68-73` treats *any* slipping answer as a valid target regardless of whether the sentence exists, so it gets picked and then renders nothing. I checked all 65,536 answer combinations (`temp/check-move.ts`):

```
picked a redirect target with NO redirectSentence: 10240 (15.6%)
culprits: [ [ 'redirect q2 opt0', 10240 ] ]
```

Those takers get "where I'd start", the reclaim paragraph, and then silence — no redirect half. Half the payoff of the quiz, missing, on a very common answer. The fix I'd make is to require the sentence for slipping answers too, which is already the documented rule for `context` ones: writing the sentence is the opt-in. Simulated it (`temp/check-move-fix.ts`) — the redirect then falls through cleanly and spreads across all six questions, `q7` 18432 / `q2` 16384 / `q4` 12288 / `q6` 5184 / `q8` 4608 / `q5` 3456, with 5184 combinations having genuinely nothing eligible. Separate from the visual work, and worth doing either way.

**The thing to notice while you look.** Drawing these forced a distinction the schema has no room for: trajectory belongs to the **area**, not the answer. "Almost no time on coaching" is a slipping *answer* about an appreciating *area* — that's why the arrow can point at it. Today `bucket` conflates the two, which is also why `q2` ended up at the head of a priority list it doesn't semantically belong in. Whichever visual you pick, that split is the change underneath it.

The numbers on both axes are mine, guessed from your copy. Argue with the pictures and I'll move them.

I need to ask for feedback on this. Help draft a short request.

1. I need to point out radar chart doesn't work when the answers aren't scored and so a radar chart would be fake.
2. Show the three ideas created and give a short explanation for each.

Here's a draft. It assumes a small group who know you (email or DM); say the word and I'll cut it to a LinkedIn version.

```
Subject: Which of these three makes the point?

I'm rebuilding the results page for my Scrum Master quiz and I'd like 60
seconds of your opinion.

The quiz doesn't score anyone. No total, no grade, no archetype. Each
answer gets classified instead: work that's getting more valuable, work
the tools are starting to do, or a constraint outside your control.

I wanted a radar chart, like every assessment on the internet has. It
doesn't work here. A radar needs a number on every axis, and I don't
have numbers, I have classifications. I'd have to invent the scores and
then present them as though I'd measured something: precise-looking
fiction. Worse, an answer like "there's no Product Owner I can
realistically coach" would plot as a low point, which reads as your
failing when it's explicitly the opposite.

So here are three attempts at a picture that shows why one area deserves
your attention more than another.

1. Transfer. Two columns: where your hours actually went on work the
tools are taking, and the work only a person can do. One arrow shows the
single change I'd make. Nothing to decode.

2. Trajectory. One vertical spectrum, from "the tools are starting to do
this" up to "only a person can do this". Every answer is a dot, sized by
how much of your time went there. The point should land before you read
a word: the big dots are all at the bottom.

3. Quadrant. How much of your time went there, against where that work
is heading. Bottom right is the drain, top right is where you want to
be, and the empty top left is the opportunity.

The positions and sizes are placeholders, so ignore the exact dots.

Two questions:
- Which one makes it obvious why to focus on one thing over another?
- Which would actually get you to change something next Sprint?
```

content.text:
Open in your browser. Four now, two profiles each:

- **A. Quadrant, plain** — four fields, your answers, axis labels only.
- **B. Quadrant, boxes named** — same plot, each corner told to you: *the people work*, *the system work*, *your own overhead*, *the coordination machine*. These name the **work**, never the person, which gets you the at-a-glance legibility an archetype buys without a label anyone has to wear.
- **C. Boxes only, no dots** — drops per-answer detail. Four named kinds of work, each filled in proportion to how much of your time landed there, arrow moving between boxes. Best on a phone; you lose the ability to point at a specific answer.
- **D. Trajectory axis** — kept, with the y-axis wording brought into line.

**Your x-axis earns its keep.** Everything the tools are taking clusters bottom-right, all of it team-coordination mechanics: running the events, the status desk, tickets and reports. The bottom-left is almost empty. So the picture says something your old balance bar could not: *the tools aren't eating your job, they're eating the coordination layer of it, and what's left is people work on one side and system work on the other.*

**One thing that needs your call, because it can make the picture lie.** You gave me a three-stop x-axis (individual → team → org) and asked for four boxes. Three stops don't halve cleanly, so "the team" ends up sitting on the divider and team-level work falls to whichever side I nudge it. Right now the divider is at *the team*, which puts team-level work on the right and produces one label I don't believe: **"the team's craft" is currently filed under *the system work*, next to org friction.** Coaching a team's engineering practices is not the same order of thing as unpicking cross-department dependencies.

Three ways out, and I'd want your read before I tune the dots any further:

1. **Move the divider to just past the team** so left is "one person and the team" and right is "beyond the team". Then the coordination machine moves to bottom-left and the bottom-right empties, which inverts the story above.
2. **Keep the divider at the team** and accept that team-level work is genuinely ambiguous, leaning on the dot labels to carry it.
3. **Go to six boxes** (2 × 3), which is what your axis actually describes. More honest, more to read.

Also, plainly: the **Transfer** visual is gone. I overwrote the file and `temp/` is gitignored (`.gitignore:36`), so it isn't recoverable. It's about forty lines to rewrite if you want it back.

content.text:
Confirmed, and the cause isn't the axis. Numbers across all 32 authored options:

```
bottom-left:   1   ← "split with delivery work" (q1 opt3, a context answer)
bottom-right:  6
top-left:     12
top-right:    13
```

Profile 1, the common full-time case, has bottom-left **completely empty**.

I assumed the two axes were correlated. They aren't: correlation between "needs a person" and scope is only −0.14. The real cause is the question set. **Only 7 of your 32 options describe work the tools are taking at all**, and six of those seven are the same thing wearing three hats: running the events, the status desk, ticket admin. All team-coordination work, all inherently team-scoped. Five of your eight questions (q4–q8) are *entirely* about work that needs a person; only the amount of attention varies. So the bottom half of any quadrant is thin, and the bottom-left is empty because no question asks about **individual-scoped work a tool can do**.

Swapping the x-axis doesn't rescue it: with "how much of your time" on x instead, bottom-left holds 2 of 32. Same hole, same reason.

Three ways out.

**1. Add a question that fills the box.** There is real individual-scoped automatable Scrum Master work, and you don't ask about any of it: preparing retro formats and agendas, building slides, writing up notes and meeting summaries, researching a facilitation technique, drafting your own updates. That's squarely "a tool does this now", it's work you do alone, and it's a question your thesis wants asked. It also makes the bottom row a genuine row rather than one lump of admin. Cost: a ninth question, and "eight questions" appears in four places in the frontmatter. **This is what I'd do** — the empty box is the picture telling you the quiz has a blind spot.

**2. Keep the hole and make it the message.** "Nothing you do on your own is what the tools are coming for." Defensible, and an empty quadrant *can* be the finding. But on a phone an empty corner reads as a rendering fault, and you've spent a quarter of the visual on it.

**3. Drop the 2×2.** With 25 of 32 options on the top half, the data is "a lot of human work at varying scope, plus one lump of team-level admin", which is not quadrant-shaped. D handles that honestly, and so does C: an empty box there is just an empty fill bar, which reads as "none of your time went here" rather than as a hole.

Worth noting whichever you pick: **C degrades gracefully and A and B don't.** If you want to keep the four boxes without adding a question, C is the only one of the three that survives the emptiness.
