content.text:
Open: `temp/quiz-result-boxes.html`. Three treatments, both profiles, and a checkbox at the top that adds the candidate ninth question live so you can watch the empty box fill.

- **C1. Equal boxes, proportional fill.** Fixed grid, a fill bar per box. An empty box has to be spoken for, so it gets its own line ("Nothing you do on your own is work a tool is taking").
- **C2. Equal boxes, listing what landed in them.** Same grid, but each box names the areas inside it, heaviest first, with a small bar each. **This recovers the per-answer detail I told you C would cost** — it turns out you only lose the scatter, not the specifics. The one move reads better here as a chip on two named items ("take time from here" / "put it here") than as an arrow between boxes.
- **C3. Mosaic, box size *is* your time.** Column widths split by where your attention went, row heights by whether that work needs a person. The distortion is the argument, and an empty box stops existing rather than needing an excuse.

Shares for the two profiles, as the boxes draw them:

```
                          people   system   overhead   machine
profile 1 (full-timer)      22%      30%        0%       48%
profile 2 (part-timer)       6%      52%       16%       26%

with the 9th question added
profile 1                   18%      25%       18%       39%
profile 2                    5%      42%       32%       21%
```

Profile 1 is the case you spotted: bottom-left at zero. C3 handles it silently, C1 and C2 have to talk about it.

Two things I'd flag:

**C3 has a failure mode C1 and C2 don't.** When a column is nearly empty the cell shrinks below the size of its own name, so I clamp it to a minimum and steal the space back from its neighbour. That means the areas stop being exactly proportional at the extremes: a taker with 5% in "the people work" sees a box drawn slightly larger than the truth. Nobody will notice, but it is a small lie baked into the shape, and it is the price of the empty box vanishing.

**The ninth question I invented for the toggle** is "How much of your time went to prep, notes and write-ups: agendas, slides, meeting summaries, your own updates?" — your wording will be better, but you can see from the numbers above that it does the job: bottom-left goes from 0% to 18% for the common case, and the bottom row stops being one lump of ticket admin.

Both pages now share `temp/quiz-model.js`, so the invented positions live in one place when you start arguing with them.

content.text:
Open. Both quiet versions, arrow gone (`curves: 0` in the render check), two tints instead of three.

What replaced the arrow: two accent words inside the relevant boxes (**"less of this"** / **"more of this"**), plus a short paragraph under each picture generated from the same numbers the boxes are drawn from, so the prose and the graphic can't drift apart. Delete the two words and each graphic still stands alone.

Other changes:

- **Bottom-left is now amber.** It sits on the bottom row, so the tools are taking it. Tinting it neutral grey was wrong. Colour now encodes one thing only, the vertical axis; left and right are carried by position and name.
- **C3 is at true proportion.** I removed the min-size clamping I flagged last time, so the areas no longer overstate a small share. Labels wrap instead, and only drop out to a caption line if the cell genuinely can't hold them.
- **C1 lost the fill-bar track, the "your time here" caption, the one-liners and the dashed empty-state.** An empty box now just fades and has no bar.

**One finding that changes my recommendation.** C3 has a structural problem I hadn't seen until the proportions were honest: *the box you're recommending is, by definition, the smallest one.* "More of this" points at the work you're currently giving least time to, so the mosaic draws it tiniest and it's first to lose its own label. On profile 2 with the ninth question added, "the people work" is 5% and can't hold a 15px label at all, so it falls out to the caption. The picture is arguing against its own recommendation.

C1 doesn't have that failure: equal boxes always hold their names, and the bar carries the proportion instead of the geometry. **I'd go with C1 quiet.** C3 is the better picture of where your time went, and the worse picture of where it should go.

content.text:
Open: `temp/quiz-result-explore.html`. Both pictures, one result set at a time.

Controls: seven presets (buried in admin, part-time and constrained, the rare case, everything in the middle, the process machine, coach with no system reach, system fixer with no people work), a **Random set** button, **All slipping** / **All gaining**, the ninth-question toggle, and a dropdown per question so you can hand-build any set. Everything redraws together, and the box shares print above the charts so you can see the numbers the pictures are made of.

I swept it before handing it over: 414 sets (all presets × both toggle states, plus 400 random) render with two charts, a reading paragraph and a move block, no broken output. Then 20,000 random sets through the model alone:

```
no reclaim target at all (nothing slipping in q3/q1/q2)   28%
no redirect target at all                                  6%
redirect picked but the sentence is MISSING (the q2 bug)   16%
the "more of this" box is under 10% of the picture         10%
```

Three things in that worth your attention:

**The q2 bug reproduces at 16%**, matching the 15.6% I measured exhaustively earlier. Independent confirmation from a different code path.

**28% "no reclaim" is not a bug**, it's the design: if nothing in q3, q1 or q2 is slipping, there is nothing to reclaim. But it means the "where I'd start" box is half-empty more often than I'd assumed. Uniform random overstates it, since real takers don't answer at random, but it's worth seeing the shape of it.

**Adding the ninth question kills the empty-box problem outright.** That 20,000-set sweep had it switched on, and not one set produced an empty box, because prep-and-write-ups always lands in bottom-left whatever you answer. Toggle it off and use the "Buried in admin" preset to see the hole come back.

**C3 still argues against itself.** Label eviction fired on 27% of the sets I rendered, and the box tagged "more of this" is under a tenth of the picture in 10% of sets. Hit **Random set** a dozen times and watch the caption line: the recommendation is the thing the mosaic draws smallest.
The challenge is that the box "your own overhead" rarely gets filled.

Worth being precise about how rarely, because it's decisive: with the current eight questions, the only answer that can put anything in that box is `q1` option 3, "The events, plus my own delivery work" — the context answer.

content.text:
Open, with a **"split the bottom row by scope (four boxes)"** toggle so you can flip between three and four. Merged, the bottom row is called *the mechanical work* ("coordination, tickets, prep, write-ups"), which is what all of it is.

I ran 2,400 sets through both layouts:

```
layout       sets   C3 label evicted   a box came out empty
3-box         607          12%                   0%
4-box         607          17%                  76%
3-box +q9     607           4%                   0%
4-box +q9     607          34%                   0%
```

That table kills my earlier recommendation. **Adding the ninth question does not rescue the four-box layout** — it just converts an empty box into an unlabellable sliver, and label eviction goes *up*, 17% to 34%. Filling a box with a thin share is not the same as the box being worth drawing.

Merging the bottom row fixes it outright, with or without the extra question: no empty box in any of the 1,214 sets, and eviction drops to 12%, or 4% once the ninth question is in.

Which puts the ninth question back where it belongs: **a content decision, not a chart decision.** Add it if "how much of your time went to prep, agendas, slides and write-ups" is a question worth asking a Scrum Master in a quiz about what AI is taking. I think it is, and the numbers say it makes the picture cleaner too, but it should no longer be load-bearing for the layout.

One consequence to weigh before you settle: merging the bottom row means the x-axis only applies to the top half. Left-versus-right stops meaning anything below the line, and "one person → wider than the team" sits under a box that spans the whole width. Honest, since the distinction genuinely isn't there, but a reader may still try to read position along the bottom row. If that bothers you, the fix is to drop the x-axis tick labels and let the two top boxes carry the distinction by name alone.

content.text:
Yes. **Nothing ever renders empty** — "nothing at all" is 0.0%, and that's zero sets, not a rounding. Every taker gets a payoff block.

But "a move" specifically is a different question, and the answer changes a lot with the two fixes:

```
                                   both    half   rare   middle  nothing
live today                        52.0%  46.1%   2.0%   0.0%   0.0%
+ eligibility fix                 65.9%  32.1%   2.0%   0.0%   0.0%
+ eligibility fix + q1 sentence   74.7%  24.0%   1.3%   0.0%   0.0%
```

**Today, 46% of takers get half a move** — usually a "reclaim the time" with nothing telling them where to put it, which is the `q2` bug. The eligibility fix alone moves 14 points of that into complete moves; the `q1` sentence another 9. The bottom row matches the mockup's coverage page exactly (74.7 / 24.0 / 1.3), which is a useful check: two independent implementations of the fix agree.

The 2.0% "rare case" is the `wellPositioned` copy, which is a legitimate result rather than a move.

Two things worth knowing before you land these:

**The `q1` sentence trims the "rare case" from 2.0% to 1.3%.** That's by design, not a regression: a `context` answer winning a half deliberately suppresses `wellPositioned`, because "not your fault" isn't "not important". The practical effect is that some part-timers who'd have been told "You're the rare case" will instead be told to reclaim time from the events. I think that's right, but it is a change in what a real group of people sees, so it should be a decision rather than a side effect.

**One small copy bug.** The `noMove` block ("You landed in the middle on every question") fires for just 16 sets out of 65,536, and on **15 of those 16 the statement is false**: those takers answered with real-world constraints, not middle answers. It's 0.02% and nowhere near worth prioritising, but if you're editing that block anyway, it wants to cover the all-context case too.
Please offer a draft of the q1 sentence.

Here it is in context, with two alternatives. The sibling to match is `q3` option 3, the other part-time `context` answer, which states the constraint and then moves straight on without sympathy or blame.

```yaml
      - text: 'The events, plus my own delivery work. The role only gets part of my week.'
        score: 0
        bucket: context
        icon: 'handsOn'
        mapSentence: 'Your hours are split between the role and delivery work, so there’s simply less Scrum Master time to spend. Judge it by what you did with the hours you had, not the ones you didn’t.'
        reclaimSentence: 'Reclaim the time. The events will fill whatever hours you give them, and you have fewer to give than most. Shorten them, hand one over, or lean on a tool, and put what you get back into the people.'
```

**A (above), the one I'd use.** "The events will fill whatever hours you give them" is the actual mechanism, and it's the reason a part-timer is hit harder than anyone else. It gives three concrete outs rather than one, which matters when the taker has least room to manoeuvre.

**B, plainer:**

> Reclaim the time. When the role only gets part of your week, running the events is the most expensive thing in it. Trim it back or lean on a tool, and put what you get back into the people.

**C, if you'd rather it name the trade explicitly:**

> Reclaim the time. Every hour the events take is an hour the people don’t get, and on a part-time week that trade is sharper. Shorten them or lean on a tool, and spend the difference on the team.

All three follow the house pattern the other three `reclaimSentence` values use: "Reclaim the time." then why this is the thing to cut, then where it goes. None of them scold, which matters here because the `mapSentence` directly above has just told this person to judge themselves on the hours they had.

One thing to watch whichever you pick: this sentence is what makes `q1` option 3 eligible, and that's what pulls the "rare case" result down from 2.0% to 1.3%. A part-timer with nothing slipping will now be told to trim the events rather than told they're doing well.

python3 - <<'PY'
import pathlib, re

p = pathlib.Path('src/content/quizzes/scrum-master-ai/index.mdx')
lines = p.read_text().split('\n')

# Which kind of work each answer puts the taker in, and roughly what share of
# their attention it implies. Order matches the options as authored.
MAP = {
 'q1': [('mechanical',0.85), ('people',0.6),  ('people',0.85), ('mechanical',0.5)],
 'q2': [('mechanical',0.7),  ('system',0.5),  ('people',0.7),  ('people',0.05)],
 'q3': [('mechanical',0.8),  ('mechanical',0.45), ('mechanical',0.1), ('mechanical',0.8)],
 'q4': [('people',0.05), ('people',0.3), ('people',0.7),  ('people',0.15)],
 'q5': [('system',0.05), ('system',0.3), ('system',0.65), ('system',0.1)],
 'q6': [('system',0.1),  ('system',0.45),('system',0.7),  ('system',0.02)],
 'q7': [('people',0.02), ('people',0.3), ('people',0.65), ('people',0.02)],
 'q8': [('system',0.02), ('system',0.3), ('system',0.7),  ('system',0.5)],
}

out, qid, opt = [], None, -1
for line in lines:
    m = re.match(r'^  - id: (\S+)\s*$', line)
    if m:
        qid, opt = m.group(1), -1
    if re.match(r'^      - text:', line):
        opt += 1
    out.append(line)
    m = re.match(r'^        bucket: (\S+)\s*$', line)
    if m and qid in MAP:
        box, weight = MAP[qid][opt]
        out.append(f"        box: {box}")
        out.append(f"        weight: {weight}")

text = '\n'.join(out)

SHAPE = """  # The lead visual. Every box is drawn at the size of the time that went to it,
  # so the picture is a map of where the hours landed and carries no number
  # anywhere. The bottom row holds a single box because the distinction does not
  # exist down there: every automatable thing a Scrum Master does is mechanical,
  # whether it is a ticket, a status round-up or a set of slides. Splitting it
  # by scope produced a box only a part-timer could ever reach.
  shape:
    label: 'Where your recent Sprints went'
    axisTop: 'needs a person'
    axisBottom: 'the tools are starting to do this'
    axisNear: 'one person'
    axisFar: 'wider than the team'
    # Two accent words in place of an arrow: nothing curves across the picture.
    tagFrom: 'less of this'
    tagTo: 'more of this'
    mostLine: 'Most of your last few Sprints went to {box}.'
    mostlyTop: 'Most of your time is already in work that needs a person.'
    mostlyBottom: 'Most of your time is in work the tools are starting to do.'
    boxes:
      - id: people
        name: 'the people work'
        row: top
        tone: valuable
      - id: system
        name: 'the system work'
        row: top
        tone: valuable
      - id: mechanical
        name: 'the mechanical work'
        row: bottom
        tone: slipping"""

old = "  balanceLabel: 'Where your recent Sprints went'"
assert old in text, 'balanceLabel not found'
text = text.replace(old, SHAPE)
p.write_text(text)
print('options annotated:', text.count('        box: '))
print('balanceLabel removed:', 'balanceLabel' not in text)

# Project History

A short, human-readable log of notable changes and the reasoning behind them.
Newest first. (Detailed, current behaviour lives in `CLAUDE.md`; this file is the
"why we did it" story.)

## 2026-07-30 — Quiz copy pass: all eight questions, one at a time

**Why.** The questions had accumulated three tics. Half of them opened "Think
about" or "Think back"; "the last couple of Sprints" appeared in three questions
plus the intro, the how-it-works strip, the section blurb, `heroBody` and
`description`, so a taker met it three times before question 1; and several
middles were hedges rather than answers, the worst being q5's bare "A bit of
both". With `randomizeOptions: 'shuffle'` on, an answer that points at its
neighbours points at whatever the shuffle put there, so every option has to read
cold with no siblings in view. Mark reviewed each question in turn and rewrote in
his own voice where the suggestion missed it.

**Two rules came out of the pass and are worth keeping.**

_Result sentences must stand alone._ The results page renders map, reclaim and
redirect sentences only; it uses the question object solely to look up an icon
(`MapMoveResults.astro`), so the question text and the answer text are never on
screen with them. Trimming a result sentence because it "repeats the question" is
therefore always wrong, and it cost q8's map line the list defining what "craft"
means before Mark caught it. De-duplicating a map line against its _own_ reclaim
line is still right: those two do render together.

_Question and answer text are the opposite case._ They are read with the question
in view, so a phrase repeated from the question stem is dead weight there.

input.old_string:
The results page leads with a **balance bar**: one flat bar whose two segments
are the proportion of `gaining` to `slipping` answers (`result.balance`), with
mixed and context answers excluded so a constraint never widens the slipping
side. It carries no number, letter or tier title, by design: the result is a map
of where the time went, not a grade. `balanceLabel` is the line above it, and
the two column headings double as its legend.

The one move is computed by `computeMapMove()` from the `mapMove` frontmatter
block:

- `reclaimPriority` — question ids in priority order; the reclaim target is the
  first eligible one.
- `redirectPriority` — same, for the redirect target (the two never collide).
- **A `context` answer can win either half of the move** if, and only if, it
  supplies that half's sentence (`reclaimSentence` / `redirectSentence`). "Not
  your fault" is not the same as "not important": some constraints are real
  problems the taker can't ignore, and leaving those in the soft context strip
  understates them. Writing the sentence is the opt-in — an author who writes one
  has decided this constraint is actionable — and it promotes the answer to the
  move, so the problem lands in the most prominent block on the page while still
  being named without blame in the map. It stays out of the slipping column and
  out of the balance either way.
input.new_string:
### The shape (the lead visual)

The results page leads with a **shape**: a two-row mosaic in which every named
kind of work is drawn at the size of the time the taker gave it. Rows are sized
by their combined share, and the boxes within a row by their share of that row,
so the areas *are* the proportions. Nothing is clamped to fit a label, and no
number appears anywhere: the result is a map of where the time went, not a grade.

Two per-option fields feed it, both independent of `bucket`:

```yaml
- text: 'Running the Scrum events and keeping everyone coordinated.'
  bucket: slipping # strength or gap
  box: mechanical # what KIND of work it is
  weight: 0.85 # roughly what share of their attention
```

`bucket` says whether the answer is a strength or a gap; `box` says what kind of
work it is. They are genuinely orthogonal: "almost no time on coaching" is a
`slipping` answer about an *appreciating* box. `weight` sizes the shape and
nothing else. It is not a score, is never summed against a maximum, and never
appears on the page. Every answered option contributes whatever its bucket,
because the shape asks "where did the time go", not "what went well" — which is
the opposite of the two map columns beside it, deliberately.

The layout is declared once:

```yaml
mapMove:
  shape:
    label: 'Where your recent Sprints went'
    axisTop: 'needs a person'
    axisBottom: 'the tools are starting to do this'
    axisNear: 'one person' # optional ends of the horizontal axis
    axisFar: 'wider than the team'
    tagFrom: 'less of this' # two or three words, in place of an arrow
    tagTo: 'more of this'
    mostLine: 'Most of your last few Sprints went to {box}.'
    mostlyTop: 'Most of your time is already in work that needs a person.'
    mostlyBottom: 'Most of your time is in work the tools are starting to do.'
    boxes:
      - { id: people, name: 'the people work', row: top, tone: valuable }
      - { id: system, name: 'the system work', row: top, tone: valuable }
      - { id: mechanical, name: 'the mechanical work', row: bottom, tone: slipping }
```

Three things about that are load-bearing.

**Name the work, never the person.** "the people work", not "the Coach". The
archetype is the thing this style refuses to hand out, and a box label is the
easiest place to smuggle one back in.

**A row may hold one box.** Putting a single box on a row says the horizontal
distinction does not exist down there. `scrum-master-ai` does that on the bottom
row: every automatable thing a Scrum Master does is mechanical whether it is a
ticket, a status round-up or a set of slides, and splitting the row by scope
produced a box only a part-timer could ever reach.

**There is no arrow.** The move is marked by `tagFrom` / `tagTo` on the two boxes
involved. A curve across the picture was hard to follow and made the whole thing
busy. `mostLine` (with `{box}` replaced by the largest box's name) and the
top/bottom line carry the reading in prose underneath; the top/bottom line is
suppressed when the largest box already sits on the majority row, because there
it only restates the sentence before it.

The component is HTML rather than SVG on purpose: an SVG's text scales with its
viewBox, so a 15px label renders at about 8px on a phone. A box too small to hold
its name hands it to a swatch-and-name key below the picture, which then lists
*every* box rather than only the missing ones — a partial list reads as an
apology and gives the reader nothing to match against. The key also carries the
move tag for any unlabelled box, because the box being recommended is by
definition the one with least time in it, so it is the smallest and the first to
lose its own label.

### The one move

The one move is computed by `computeMapMove()` from the `mapMove` frontmatter
block:

- `reclaimPriority` — question ids in priority order; the reclaim target is the
  first eligible one.
- `redirectPriority` — same, for the redirect target (the two never collide).
- **An answer is eligible for a half of the move only if it supplies that half's
  sentence** (`reclaimSentence` / `redirectSentence`). Requiring it is what stops
  the walk dying on a high-priority answer that has no copy for this half: before
  the rule applied to `slipping` answers too, `scrum-master-ai`'s "status and
  logistics desk" (first in `redirectPriority`, with a `reclaimSentence` but no
  `redirectSentence`) won the redirect on 16% of answer sets and then rendered
  nothing, so takers were told what to stop doing and never told where the time
  should go.
- **That also lets a `context` answer win either half.** "Not your fault" is not
  the same as "not important": some constraints are real problems the taker can't
  ignore, and leaving those in the soft context strip understates them. Writing
  the sentence is the opt-in — an author who writes one has decided this
  constraint is actionable — and it promotes the answer to the move, so the
  problem lands in the most prominent block on the page while still being named
  without blame in the map. It stays out of the slipping column either way.

input.old_string: **Two result styles.** The engine supports two pluggable results renderers, selected per quiz via `resultStyle`. `band` is the "you scored X, you're a Y" style (`ai-failure-modes` used it). `map-move` is the reflective, per-answer style: each option carries a `bucket` (`gaining` / `mixed` / `slipping` / `context`) and per-answer sentences, and a `mapMove` frontmatter block holds the move-selection priorities plus all the surrounding copy; `computeMapMove()` picks the one reclaim + redirect move. **Two result styles.** The engine supports two pluggable results renderers, selected per quiz via `resultStyle`. `band` is the "you scored X, you're a Y" style (`ai-failure-modes` used it). `map-move` is the reflective, per-answer style: each option carries a `bucket` (`gaining` / `mixed` / `slipping` / `context`) and per-answer sentences, and a `mapMove` frontmatter block holds the move-selection priorities plus all the surrounding copy; `computeMapMove()` picks the one reclaim + redirect move. A `map-move` result page carries **no number, letter or tier title anywhere**: it's a map of where the time went, not a grade. That was a hard requirement, so don't reintroduce a score, a band headline or an archetype label. `mapMove.framing` still exists but is no longer printed; it survives only to give `levelTagPrefix` a tier to tag with. `context` answers (e.g. part-time role, no PO to coach) are named but never scored as gaps. **An answer wins a half of the move only if it carries that half's sentence** (`reclaimSentence` / `redirectSentence`). That is what lets a `context` answer win one, because "not your fault" is not the same as "not important": a missing Product Owner, impediments that never surface, or admin that doesn't shrink just because the role is part-time are all real problems, and the soft context strip understates them. Writing the sentence is the opt-in — an author who writes one has decided the constraint is actionable; without it the answer stays in the context strip. `scrum-master-ai` uses this on q1 and q3 (reclaim), q2, q6 and q7 (redirect). Such an answer stays out of the slipping column, and it also suppresses the `wellPositioned` fallback (which renders _instead_ of the move, so it would otherwise hide the problem). The same rule applies to `slipping` answers, which is what stops the priority walk dying on an answer with no copy for that half (see `HISTORY.md`, 2026-08-04). The current live quiz (`scrum-master-ai`) uses `map-move`. See the engine README for the authoring guide.

**The shape (the `map-move` lead visual).** The page leads with a two-row mosaic (`MapMoveShape.astro`) in which every named kind of work is drawn at the size of the time the taker gave it: rows sized by their combined share, boxes within a row by their share of that row. It replaced a two-segment balance bar, which could only say "this much of your time was well spent" and never which kinds of work the time went to. Two per-option fields feed it, both **independent of `bucket`**: `box` (which kind of work) and `weight` (roughly what share of attention, 0..1, never a score and never printed). `bucket` says strength-or-gap; `box` says what kind of work — "almost no time on coaching" is a `slipping` answer about an appreciating box. The layout is declared in `mapMove.shape`. Three rules: **name the work, never the person** (a box label is the easiest place to smuggle an archetype back in); **a row may hold one box**, which says the horizontal distinction doesn't exist on that row (`scrum-master-ai`'s bottom row is one box, because every automatable thing a Scrum Master does is mechanical, and splitting it by scope produced a box only a part-timer could reach); and **there is no arrow** — the move is marked by `tagFrom` / `tagTo` on the two boxes. It's HTML, not SVG, because an SVG's text scales with its viewBox and would render at ~8px on a phone. A box too small for its name hands it to a swatch key below, which then lists every box (a partial list reads as an apology) and carries the move tag for any unlabelled box, since the recommended box is by definition the smallest.

input.command:
python3 - <<'PY'
import pathlib
p = pathlib.Path('HISTORY.md')
s = p.read_text()
anchor = '## 2026-07-30 — Quiz copy pass'
entry = '''## 2026-08-04 — Quiz results: a shape instead of a balance bar, and the move stops going silent

**Why.** The `map-move` results page led with a two-segment balance bar: the
proportion of gaining to slipping answers. It could say "this much of your time
was well spent" and nothing else, so it could not answer the question the page
exists to answer, which is why one area deserves attention ahead of another.

A radar chart was the first idea and was wrong, for a reason worth writing down:
**a radar needs a number on every axis, and this quiz deliberately has none.**
Answers are classified, not scored. Drawing one would have meant inventing the
numbers and then presenting them as measurement, and a `context` answer ("there
is no Product Owner I can coach") would have plotted as a low point, reading as
the taker's failing when the whole design says it is not.

**What replaced it.** A two-row mosaic where each named kind of work is drawn at
the size of the time that went to it. Two new per-option fields feed it, `box`
and `weight`, both independent of `bucket`: the bucket says strength-or-gap, the
box says what kind of work, and those are genuinely orthogonal ("almost no time
on coaching" is a slipping answer about an appreciating box). Areas are exact,
nothing is clamped to fit a label, and there is still no number on the page.

**Three things fell out of building it, each worth keeping.**

_A quadrant needed a fourth box that could not exist._ Splitting the bottom row
by scope (one person versus wider than the team) produced "your own overhead",
which exactly one option in thirty-two could reach, and only if the taker was
part-time. For a full-timer the box was not rare, it was unreachable. Adding a
ninth question to fill it made things worse, not better: it converted an empty
box into an unlabellable sliver and pushed label eviction from 17% to 34%. The
fix was to stop splitting the row. Every automatable thing a Scrum Master does is
mechanical, whether it is a ticket, a status round-up or a set of slides.

_The arrow had to go._ A curve from the box to take time from to the box to put
it into was hard to follow and made the picture busy. Two accent words on the two
boxes say the same thing and nothing crosses the picture.

_The recommended box is always the smallest._ "More of this" points at the work
the taker has given least time to, so it is the smallest box and the first to
lose its own label. The key below the picture therefore carries the move tag for
any unlabelled box, or the most important annotation on the page would disappear
in exactly the cases it matters.

**The bug this uncovered.** `eligible()` in `map-move.ts` accepted any `slipping`
answer for a half of the move whether or not a sentence existed for that half.
`q2`'s "status and logistics desk" sits first in `redirectPriority` and has a
`reclaimSentence` but no `redirectSentence`, so on **16% of all answer sets** it
won the redirect and then rendered nothing: the taker was told what to stop doing
and never told where the time should go. Worse, once the shape existed it also
put "more of this" on the mechanical work, which is advice to spend more time on
the coordination machine. Requiring the sentence (already the rule for `context`
answers) makes the walk carry on to the next candidate that has something to say.

Measured over all 65,536 answer sets, complete moves went from 52.0% to 65.9%,
and a new `reclaimSentence` on `q1`'s part-time answer took it to 74.7%. Nothing
ever renders empty, before or after.

'''
p.write_text(s.replace(anchor, entry + anchor, 1))
print('entry added:', '2026-08-04' in p.read_text())

Both done. `astro check` 0 errors / 0 warnings / 0 hints across 158 files, `lint:tw` clean, production build exits 0.

**The eligibility fix** (`map-move.ts:68-88`): an answer wins a half of the move only if it carries that half's sentence. That was already the rule for `context` answers; extending it to `slipping` is what makes the priority walk continue past `q2` instead of dying on it.

**The results page** now leads with `MapMoveShape.astro` in place of the balance bar: the three-box mosaic at true proportion you picked, no arrow, two tints, the move marked with "less of this" / "more of this".

New engine surface, all APR-agnostic:

- Two per-option fields, `box` and `weight`, deliberately independent of `bucket`. The bucket says strength-or-gap, the box says what kind of work. That split is what makes the picture possible: "almost no time on coaching" is a `slipping` answer about an appreciating box.
- A `mapMove.shape` block holding the layout and every word on the picture.
- The component is HTML, not SVG. An SVG's text scales with its viewBox, so a 15px label renders at about 8px on a phone.

Over all 65,536 answer sets: complete moves **52.0% → 74.7%**, shares sum to 1 to within 4e-16, and nothing ever renders empty.

Two things I decided and you should overrule if you disagree:

- **The label thresholds are set for a phone, not a desktop.** A box hands its name to the key below when it's under 26% of its row or its row is under 10% of the whole. That fires on 32% of results. Tuning to desktop would drop it to about 10%, at the cost of clipped labels on the more common device. When the key appears it lists *all three* boxes with swatches, and it carries the move tag for any unlabelled box, because the recommended box is by definition the smallest one on the picture.
- **`mostlyTop` / `mostlyBottom` only print when the largest box is on the opposite row from the majority.** Otherwise it restated the sentence before it: "Most of your Sprints went to the mechanical work. Most of your time is in work the tools are starting to do."

Still open:

- **The weights are mine.** All 32 of them, guessed from your copy. They're the one thing in this that isn't grounded in something you wrote.
- **The `noMove` copy bug** from earlier is untouched: it fires on 16 sets and is factually false on 15 of them.
- `temp/quiz-result-visuals.html` and `temp/quiz-result-boxes.html` are superseded and drifting; say the word and I'll delete them. The explore and coverage pages still work.

I killed the dev server after opening those three result pages, so `npm run dev` again if you want to poke at more. Not committed.

1. Delete the unused html files.
2. Suggest a fix for the noMove copy bug
3. I think I would prefer the C1 approach where the boxes are fixed sized and there is a line/bar illustrating how much their doing.

lines: **Two result styles.** The engine supports two pluggable results renderers, selected per quiz via `resultStyle`. `band` is the "you scored X, you're a Y" style (`ai-failure-modes` used it). `map-move` is the reflective, per-answer style: each option carries a `bucket` (`gaining` / `mixed` / `slipping` / `context`) and per-answer sentences, and a `mapMove` frontmatter block holds the move-selection priorities plus all the surrounding copy; `computeMapMove()` picks the one reclaim + redirect move. A `map-move` result page carries **no number, letter or tier title anywhere**: it's a map of where the time went, not a grade. That was a hard requirement, so don't reintroduce a score, a band headline or an archetype label. `mapMove.framing` still exists but is no longer printed; it survives only to give `levelTagPrefix` a tier to tag with. `context` answers (e.g. part-time role, no PO to coach) are named but never scored as gaps. **An answer wins a half of the move only if it carries that half's sentence** (`reclaimSentence` / `redirectSentence`). That is what lets a `context` answer win one, because "not your fault" is not the same as "not important": a missing Product Owner, impediments that never surface, or admin that doesn't shrink just because the role is part-time are all real problems, and the soft context strip understates them. Writing the sentence is the opt-in — an author who writes one has decided the constraint is actionable; without it the answer stays in the context strip. `scrum-master-ai` uses this on q1 and q3 (reclaim), q2, q6 and q7 (redirect). Such an answer stays out of the slipping column, and it also suppresses the `wellPositioned` fallback (which renders _instead_ of the move, so it would otherwise hide the problem). The same rule applies to `slipping` answers, which is what stops the priority walk dying on an answer with no copy for that half (see `HISTORY.md`, 2026-08-04). 12	exists to answer, which is why one area deserves attention ahead of another.
13	
14	A radar chart was the first idea and was wrong, for a reason worth writing down:
15	**a radar needs a number on every axis, and this quiz deliberately has none.**
16	Answers are classified, not scored. Drawing one would have meant inventing the
17	numbers and then presenting them as measurement, and a `context` answer ("there
18	is no Product Owner I can coach") would have plotted as a low point, reading as
19	the taker's failing when the whole design says it is not.
20	
21	**What replaced it.** A fixed grid of named kinds of work, each carrying a bar
22	showing how much of the taker's time went to it. Two new per-option fields feed
23	it, `box` and `weight`, both independent of `bucket`: the bucket says
24	strength-or-gap, the box says what kind of work, and those are genuinely
25	orthogonal ("almost no time on coaching" is a slipping answer about an
26	appreciating box). There is still no number on the page.
27	
28	**The mosaic that lost, and why it matters.** The first build drew each box at
29	the actual size of its share, which is a better picture of where the time went
30	and was the version everyone preferred on sight. It failed on the case the page
31	exists for. The box being recommended is by definition the one the taker has
32	given least time to, so it was always the smallest box on the picture and always
33	the first too small to hold its own label. Label thresholds, a fallback key
34	below the picture, and finally the move tag migrating into that key were all
35	machinery to paper over a picture arguing against its own recommendation. Fixed
36	boxes plus a bar say the same thing about proportion and guarantee every box can
37	be read. Worth knowing before anyone rebuilds the mosaic.
38	
39	**Three more things fell out of building it, each worth keeping.**
40	
41	_A quadrant needed a fourth box that could not exist._ Splitting the bottom row
42	by scope (one person versus wider than the team) produced "your own overhead",
43	which exactly one option in thirty-two could reach, and only if the taker was
44	part-time. For a full-timer the box was not rare, it was unreachable. Adding a
45	ninth question to fill it made things worse, not better: it converted an empty
46	box into an unlabellable sliver and pushed label eviction from 17% to 34%. The
47	fix was to stop splitting the row. Every automatable thing a Scrum Master does is
48	mechanical, whether it is a ticket, a status round-up or a set of slides.
49	
50	_The arrow had to go._ A curve from the box to take time from to the box to put
51	it into was hard to follow and made the picture busy. Two accent words on the two
52	boxes say the same thing and nothing crosses the picture.
53	
54	**The bug this uncovered.** `eligible()` in `map-move.ts` accepted any `slipping`
55	answer for a half of the move whether or not a sentence existed for that half.
56	`q2`'s "status and logistics desk" sits first in `redirectPriority` and has a
57	`reclaimSentence` but no `redirectSentence`, so on **16% of all answer sets** it
58	won the redirect and then rendered nothing: the taker was told what to stop doing
59	and never told where the time should go. Worse, once the shape existed it also
60	put "more of this" on the mechanical work, which is advice to spend more time on
61	the coordination machine. Requiring the sentence (already the rule for `context`
62	answers) makes the walk carry on to the next candidate that has something to say.
63	
64	Measured over all 65,536 answer sets, complete moves went from 52.0% to 65.9%,
65	and a new `reclaimSentence` on `q1`'s part-time answer took it to 74.7%. Nothing
66	ever renders empty, before or after.
67	
68	## 2026-07-30 — Quiz copy pass: all eight questions, one at a time
69	
70	**Why.** The questions had accumulated three tics. Half of them opened "Think
71	about" or "Think back"; "the last couple of Sprints" appeared in three questions
72	plus the intro, the how-it-works strip, the section blurb, `heroBody` and
73	`description`, so a taker met it three times before question 1; and several
74	middles were hedges rather than answers, the worst being q5's bare "A bit of
75	both". With `randomizeOptions: 'shuffle'` on, an answer that points at its
76	neighbours points at whatever the shuffle put there, so every option has to read
77	cold with no siblings in view. Mark reviewed each question in turn and rewrote in
78	his own voice where the suggestion missed it.
79	
80	**Two rules came out of the pass and are worth keeping.**
81	
82	_Result sentences must stand alone._ The results page renders map, reclaim and
83	redirect sentences only; it uses the question object solely to look up an icon
84	(`MapMoveResults.astro`), so the question text and the answer text are never on
85	screen with them. Trimming a result sentence because it "repeats the question" is
86	therefore always wrong, and it cost q8's map line the list defining what "craft"
87	means before Mark caught it. De-duplicating a map line against its _own_ reclaim
88	line is still right: those two do render together.
89	
90	_Question and answer text are the opposite case._ They are read with the question
91	in view, so a phrase repeated from the question stem is dead weight there.
92	
93	**Two factual errors, not style.** q3's part-time answer claimed a part-time
94	Scrum Master has less admin. The load comes from the team existing, so it is the
95	same either way and lands in fewer hours, which makes it worse. And q6's slipping
96	map said the impediment "sat there or got worked around" when working around it
97	is a _different answer_ in the same question, so it told people they had done
98	something they hadn't.
99	
100	**Two outright bugs:** q7's map had a stray comma between subject and verb plus a
101	dropped "of the" ("is one earliest and most important activities"), and q4's
102	redirect sentence had no full stop.
103	
104	**Vocabulary.** Mark never says "blocker", always "impediment". That word had
105	leaked into two questions, two answers and an icon name; the icon rename reached
106	`QuizIcon.tsx` and the engine README. "Sprint" is capitalised throughout, in the
107	quiz and in the CTA copy that quotes it. `PO` is spelled out everywhere, because
108	shuffled options mean there is no stable first use to define an abbreviation
109	against.
110	
111	**One priority change with real effect.** `redirectPriority` now leads with `q2`.
112	If nobody brings the Scrum Master anything, finding out why sits upstream of
113	every coaching gap below it: you cannot coach people who do not come to you, so
114	"put the time into coaching" is not yet actionable advice for that person.
115	
116	**Two more engine features fell out of it.** A `context` answer can now win the
117	**reclaim**, not just the redirect, on the same opt-in: supply that half's
118	sentence or stay in the context strip. The part-timer drowning in admin is
119	exactly who most needs "reclaim the admin time" and could never be given it,
120	because reclaim was slipping-only. `wellPositioned` had to learn about it too, or
121	it renders instead of the move and swallows the result. And `label` on a question
122	supplies the eyebrow text where there is no section to supply it.
123	
124	**Comments came out.** Mark almost never writes them, and every comment in the
125	repo was generated rather than authored; a needed comment usually means the work
126	is badly framed. The five added to the quiz frontmatter during this work were
127	removed, which is why the reasoning above lives here instead.

All three done.

**1. Deleted** `temp/quiz-result-visuals.html` and `temp/quiz-result-boxes.html`. The explore and coverage pages remain and still work.

**2. The `noMove` copy bug.** The 15 false cases are all the same shape: every answer was mixed or context, with at least one context answer, and no context answer carried a sentence for its half. So they *didn't* land in the middle on every question — they named real constraints. It's a one-sentence rewrite, no code, because a second frontmatter field and a branch is too much machinery for 16 answer sets out of 65,536:

```yaml
  noMove: |
    Nothing you said stands out enough for me to point at. Either your answers
    landed in the middle, or the things that did stand out are outside your
    control. Start with whichever question was hardest to answer.
```

That covers both routes in and is shorter than what's there. Not applied — you asked for a suggestion, and it's your copy.

**3. Switched the shape to C1.** Fixed boxes, each with a bar. This deleted a whole class of problem rather than just changing the look: with equal boxes every box always holds its own name, so the size thresholds, the fallback key, the swatch legend and the tag-in-key workaround are all gone. The move tags now always render inside their box.

One thing that needed care: a row holding one box makes that box twice as wide as a box in a row of two, so an unscaled bar would draw a 24% share the same length as a 48% one. Bars are scaled by their row's box count. Verified live — mechanical at 48% draws 2.14× the length of people at 22%, against a share ratio of 2.18, the residual being identical padding in boxes of different widths.

Rendered checks against the dev server: 200s across four answer sets, shares correct, both tags present wherever a move exists, none where it doesn't. `astro check` 0/0/0 across 159 files, `lint:tw` clean, production build exits 0.

Docs updated in three places, and all three now record that the true-proportion mosaic was **built and rejected**, with the reason: the recommended box is by definition the smallest, so it was always the first too small to hold its label and the picture argued against its own recommendation. Worth having written down before someone rebuilds it.

Two notes:

- I removed the six lines of comment I'd added to the quiz frontmatter. `HISTORY.md` records that frontmatter comments were deliberately stripped on 2026-07-30 with the reasoning moved into the log, and mine now duplicated three other places. I also fixed a pre-existing frontmatter comment that still described the balance bar.
- **`git status` shows changes I didn't make**: the course components, the course content files, `src/content.config.ts` and a new `src/lib/courses.ts`. Those are yours, untouched by me, and nothing above covers them.

Not committed.

31	### Post-course newsletter signup (prefilled Cakemail form)
32	
33	Post-course emails sent by `email-automation/` include a "Subscribe to the Newsletter" link pointing at `/newsletter-subscribe/` (`src/pages/newsletter-subscribe.astro`) with the student's details prefilled in the query string: `?email=…&custom_attributes[firstname]=…&auto_submit=1`. That page embeds a Cakemail form bound to the Newsletter Subscribers list (double opt-in); Cakemail's `form-prefill.js` reads the params off the page URL, fills the form, and auto-submits it. The link is built by `buildPrefillSignupUrl()` in `email-automation/src/signup-url.ts`.
34	
35	There is **no server-side endpoint, HMAC signature, or OAuth token** in this path (it predates and is separate from the Turnstile gate below). Double opt-in is the abuse guard: a forged link can only send a confirmation email to the address that owns it, which never subscribes without the click. This prefilled-link path stays fully client-side; the general newsletter form, the AI forms, and the quiz instead route through the Turnstile-gated `/api/newsletter-signup` endpoint (see "Signup bot protection" below).
36	
37	The Newsletter Subscribers list ID is not a secret and lives in `shared/cakemail-constants.ts` as `NEWSLETTER_SUBSCRIBERS_LIST_ID`.
38	
39	### Signup bot protection: Turnstile gate (`/api/newsletter-signup`)
40	
41	All browser signups except the post-course prefilled link (the general newsletter form, both AI lead-magnet forms, and the quiz capture) POST same-origin to `/api/newsletter-signup` (`src/pages/api/newsletter-signup.ts`, `prerender = false` so it deploys as a Netlify function). The function verifies a **Cloudflare Turnstile** token and only then forwards the multipart submission to one consolidated Cakemail hosted form, server-side. This replaced the old browser-direct POSTs, which exposed the raw Cakemail form URL in the client bundle where bots scraped it and submitted junk (a client-side honeypot never sees a direct POST).
42	
43	- **Turnstile keys are static (no rotation).** Public site key: a constant in `src/constants/turnstile.ts` (baked into the client bundle — a `PUBLIC_` env var would offer no advantage). Secret: Netlify env `TURNSTILE_SECRET_KEY`, read at runtime via `process.env` so a key change needs no redeploy. **No Cakemail credentials** are involved — the hosted form accepts anonymous POSTs, so the function only verifies + forwards (this is why it's set-and-forget, unlike the old OAuth path).
44	- **The Cakemail form URL is server-only:** `src/lib/server/cakemail-forms.ts` (`CAKEMAIL_FORM_URL` + `cakemailFormUrlFor()`), removed from `shared/cakemail-constants.ts` so it never reaches the browser. One consolidated form serves every purpose; the client sends a `form` field (`newsletter` | `ai` | `quiz`) that currently all map to the one URL but leave room to split a purpose back onto its own form.
45	- **Shared widget:** `src/components/global/turnstile.tsx` (`<Turnstile onToken onExpire ref>`; loads the script once per page, explicit render). Each form keeps a `token` + `submitError`, blocks submit until a token exists, appends `cf-turnstile-response` + `form`, and resets the widget on failure. The submission is now same-origin (not `no-cors`), so the form reads the real response.
46	
47	### Self-hosted quiz engine (`src/lib/quiz-engine/`)
48	
49	Quizzes are authored as MDX files in `src/content/quizzes/{slug}/index.mdx` and rendered by a small, self-contained engine in `src/lib/quiz-engine/`. The engine is designed to be extractable to a standalone open-source Astro package later, so it has no imports from APR-specific code. See `src/lib/quiz-engine/README.md` for the engine's public API and authoring guide.
50	
51	Routes (APR-specific, consume the engine):
52	
53	- `/quiz/{slug}/` — landing page (`src/pages/quiz/[slug].astro`). Renders hero + category cards + persuasion block from frontmatter, then mounts the React `QuizStepper` island.
54	- `/quiz/{slug}/results/` — results page (`src/pages/quiz/[slug]/results.astro`, SSR). Dispatches on the quiz's `resultStyle` frontmatter field (`'band'` | `'map-move'`, default `'band'`). **Band** reads `?total=&max=&level=&{sectionId}={level}` and renders the matching `<ResultCard>` blocks from the quiz's MDX body. **Map-move** reads the raw answers from a single `?a=` param and renders the `MapMoveResults.astro` engine component (a per-answer map + one recommended move) directly from frontmatter, not the MDX body. Both query strings are intentionally unsigned: anyone can craft a URL to view a tier/result. If tamper-resistance becomes important, sign the query in the browser before redirect and verify on the page.
55

content.text:
Three, none of them flattering. Start `npm run dev` first.

**1. The common case: buried in the machine**

```
http://localhost:4321/quiz/scrum-master-ai/results/?a=q1-0.q2-0.q3-0.q4-1.q5-1.q6-1.q7-0.q8-1
```

63% mechanical work, and **nothing at all in the gaining column** — four slipping answers, zero strengths. This is the harshest thing the page can say to someone, and it's the modal result. Ask: does it land as useful, or as a telling-off?

**2. Part-time and constrained**

```
http://localhost:4321/quiz/scrum-master-ai/results/?a=q1-3.q2-1.q3-3.q4-3.q5-1.q6-0.q7-3.q8-2
```

Four of the eight answers are `context`: shared role, no Product Owner, impediments that never surface. The move here is won *by* a context answer, which is the mechanism you deliberately built. Ask: does the page make a structural constraint feel like a personal failing? That's the one thing this design is most at risk of getting wrong, and only someone actually in that position will tell you.

**3. Half a move**

```
http://localhost:4321/quiz/scrum-master-ai/results/?a=q1-0.q2-2.q3-2.q4-1.q5-1.q6-1.q7-2.q8-2
```

Someone doing well on the people work but still running the events. There's a reclaim and **no redirect**, because nothing in the redirect list came back as a gap. So they're told what to stop doing and never told where the time goes. That's 24% of all results, it's the page's weakest state, and it's the one I'd most want strangers' eyes on.

I skipped the "rare case" (everything already in the people work) and the all-middle set. The first is the flattering one; the second fires on 16 answer sets and hits the `noMove` copy bug you haven't decided on yet.

**To actually send these to friends** you'd need a Netlify deploy preview, which means a branch and a push. I haven't done that. If you want it, push the branch and Netlify will give you a preview URL with the same paths.
FIX THE NOMove bug I have asked repeatedly.
